Sep 16 01:45Z note: the Largest-Company tab re-baked on the Sep 15 finals and a fresh twenty-book walk (eight September rows added to its table and sep3NVDA re-marked, 145 → 153 rows carrying RV); its best lines — Sep Apple crown 1.66×, dec-AAPL 1.46×, sep2NVDA 1.61× on a $106 book — all sit UNDER this board’s 2.00× cut, so the top 50 below is unchanged; the “best unconditional lines below the cut” are now those, and the two Analysis figures quoted in the footnote (dec-AAPL 1.31×, dec-MSFT 1.02×) read 1.46× / 1.29× on the Sep 16 bake. The model values are NOT re-baked — that is what “relative value” means here: the Analysis fairs (as ranked on Sep 15) are the Sep 12 quadrature on the Sep 11 closes, the Treasuries fairs the Sep 10 re-bake on the Sep 9 close, the Oil conditionals the Sep 10 bootstrap, Bitcoin the Sep 1 bake, Iran the Sep 1 conditional inputs; the one moving part inside a fair is the odds-space lift the Oil and Treasuries conditional books define for their LIFT and INPUT rows, which by construction is re-applied to tonight’s mid (a re-marked market carries its own likelihood ratio with it). Seventeen rows are off the board: sixteen whose markets have resolved on or since Sep 10 (Gamma closed=true, every one YES) — the 10Y 4.85 / 4.88 / 4.91 / 4.94 / 4.97 September rungs (4.97 closed Sep 14 on the 4.97 Treasury.gov print), 5Y 4.78, 30Y 5.33, the 6.75% PMMS mortgage rung, WTI $100 HIGH and $100 LOW in September and the $90 HIGH that had resolved earlier, gold $4,300 LOW, DXY 99.50 HIGH — and one (Iran targets Oman by Sep 30) whose book came back empty with no Gamma market behind its token, held off pending a token check. Four bases share the board and are labeled on every row: MODEL rows are unconditional — the tab’s own model against tonight’s price — while IF INVASION rows are the Iran tab’s conditional values, worth their RV ONLY if a US ground offensive launches (the market prices that trigger at 16.5¢ tonight), IF 10Y 5.00 rows are the Treasuries tab’s conditional book, worth their RV only if the 10-year prints 5.00% on Treasury.gov before Dec 31 (priced 95.9¢ tonight after the Sep 14 print of 4.97 and a 4.985 evening quote — the scenario is all but the trigger itself, so these rows now read almost unconditionally), and IF BRENT 130 rows are the Oil tab’s conditional book, worth their RV only if the front-month Brent contract trades $130 at any point by Oct 1 (the Oil tab’s Sep 10 18.6%; Brent Nov quoted 106.70 tonight, 2.4% under the 109.29 the tab was built on, with twelve sessions left through Sep 30). Reading the board. The raw sort answers “how much of a favorite does each side’s own model think it is, per dollar at tonight’s mid” — nothing more. It does NOT answer “what should I buy”: 49 of the 50 rows need their trigger to fire before their RV means anything — the 27 IF-INVASION rows need the invasion (multiply by the trigger’s 16.5% for the unconditional view and almost all of them drop below 2× — the 33× at #1 is a 40¢ conditional on a 1.2¢ ticket, the purest scenario lottery on the board), the 21 IF-BRENT-130 rows need a $130 front-month Brent print by Oct 1 (the Oil tab’s 18.6% on Sep 10, with Brent 2.4% lower tonight and twelve sessions left; multiply through and only the $120 / $125 / $130 WTI rungs clear their mids (scenario value × 18.6% = 18.0 / 11.9 / 6.7 against 14.35 / 7.0 / 4.75), and that on a Sep 10 touch probability Brent’s slide since argues is lower; most of the ladder also trades under the tab’s Sep 10 unconditional numbers, which are Sep 10 model numbers, not fresh ones), and the 1 IF-10Y-5.00 row needs a Treasury.gov 10 Yr print of 5.00 before Dec 31 (priced 95.9% tonight, the 10-year at 4.985 — so its conditional is nearly the unconditional); they are ranked here at the mid like every other row, while the conditional tables rank them at the ask; the model rows carry their tabs’ own disagreements (the Bitcoin rows ride the Sep 1 bake against tonight’s mids; dec-AAPL’s Sep 12 fair against a mid that has walked from 13.75 to 23.4); and RV says nothing about BOOKS — the Market? column is carried through precisely because a 2.1× on $28 of bids (#48, the only MODEL row on the board) is a smaller fact than a 1.5× on $5,000. The board’s honest headline after the Sep 15 re-mark: the site’s best unconditional, deep-book line is BTC reach $110k · Dec at 1.61× on a Sep 1 fair, below the cut, with Apple largest company · Dec 31 at 1.31× on a Sep 12 fair the market has mostly caught up to — and everything ranked above them is conditional, on a thin book, or both — which is exactly why the deep-book qualifier is in the sentence. The deep conditional rows tonight are the Iran-airspace YES ($3,371 of asks within five points of the 9 ask; Iran tab 85, Oil tab 35) and the WTI $115 / $120 rungs ($2,899 and $516 within five points of the ask); the Oil tab’s ceasefire NOs that were the deep books on Sep 10 are still deep ($60,953 of YES bids within five points on the Sep 30 leg) but no longer cheap — the ceasefire holding moved the book to 91.5 and the re-lift to 23.7.

Largest Company on Earth — Odds vs. Reality

Polymarket runs books on which company finishes as the world's largest by market cap. This tab now tracks August 31, September 30 and December 31, 2026 — the July block was resolved (NVIDIA) and has been retired from the tab in favour of the live September ladder. This page compares live Polymarket odds against a probability model driven by the actual market-cap gap, flags where the odds don't reflect reality, and measures how fast the odds move. Aug 1, 2026 — model correction: the fair column now prices the event these books actually resolve on, P(this company is the largest), computed by quadrature over the same diffusion. It used to price P(this company passes today's leader) and back out the leader as a residual — a union bound that double-counted overtakes and understated the leader by 6 pts in August and 24.5 pts in December. Every edge on this page is restated below; the flagship +31.7 was an artifact. Live prices pull from the Polymarket CLOB API and Finnhub every 60 seconds.

"Credible reporting" is measurably fuzzy — August re-runs the game

Idea added Jul 26, 2026 · Reviewed Aug 28, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

The de facto scoreboard traders cite is companiesmarketcap.com — and in late July it was internally inconsistent by hundreds of billions (front page vs detail pages carrying May share counts). At July’s 7% gap it didn’t matter, and at tonight’s 12.12% closing crown gap it still doesn’t — though Friday’s −4.58% NVDA session is the reminder that clearances are rented, not owned: $327B of the record 19.41% cushion left in one day. The seats: Apple holds #2 by 11.28% over Alphabet ($475.9B). Compute price × latest 10-Q share count yourself; don’t trust aggregators near the wire. Known quirks in these specific books — one fired on resolution night

Idea added Jul 26, 2026 · Reviewed Aug 28, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

• The SpaceX July-cap band market demonstrated the class of risk this card exists for: a "sits mid-range" consensus mark hid a close that broke the band — the NO this page priced as a zero paid ≈par (the account sold 98.0–99.0¢; ledger row 63). Cap prints near band edges are exactly where "credible reporting" wobbles. • Aramco’s exchange (Tadawul) trades Sun–Thu — its month-end number is Thursday’s close. • Share counts: Apple retires ~2.5%/yr via buybacks between 10-Qs; a sub-0.5% finish can flip on which count a source uses. • Alphabet = all classes (A+B+C). • The August book still carries unopened "Company A–P" placeholder markets at 50¢ with zero liquidity — not tradable, not part of the sum.

Live plumbing on this page

Idea added Jul 26, 2026 · Reviewed Aug 28, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

Odds: Polymarket CLOB GET /midpoint?token_id=… per contract (no auth, CORS-open) every 60s. Caps: Finnhub quotes × fixed share counts, refreshed on the same tick. Model fair values, edges and verdict badges recompute client-side on every refresh. As of Aug 1 the fair column is exact-rank: each name carries idiosyncratic log-vol σ/√2 (so any pair’s log-ratio keeps the published σ = 2%/day, and any common market factor cancels in a ranking), and P(X is the largest) is integrated over X’s own shock by 481-node Simpson quadrature on [−8, 8] — about 1 ms per book. It replaces the pairwise construction (challenger = P(chal > leader), leader = 100 − Σ), which was a union bound and understated the leader by 6.3 pts in August and 24.5 in December. Trading-day countdown with the US holiday calendar is unchanged. Once the July markets settle on-chain their midpoint endpoints go dark — the July rows above then hold tonight’s baked terminal prints permanently. If either API is unreachable the page falls back to the baked snapshot and the pill in the header flips from LIVE to SNAPSHOT.

Methodology & Honest Caveats

Model change, Aug 1 2026 — read this first. Until tonight the fair column answered the wrong question. It priced each challenger as P(chal ends above today’s leader) = Φ(ln(capchal/caplead) / σ√T) and then defined the leader’s own leg as 100 − Σ(challengers) − small legs. These books do not resolve on “did you pass the leader”; they resolve on “are you the largest”. The two differ because the passing events overlap — one bad quarter for the leader pushes several challengers past at once — so Σ(challengers) is a union bound that overstates P(someone passes), and the entire error landed in the residual. Measured bias: the leader leg read 6.3 pts low in August and 24.5 pts low in December, and the challengers carried an equal and opposite error (December: Apple +9.2, Alphabet +10.9, Microsoft +3.8, Amazon +0.6 — summing to exactly the leader’s 24.5), which is where the page’s long-running “+31.7 on NVIDIA-December” came from. The replacement keeps the identical diffusion and the identical published σ, and just does the integral. Each name gets idiosyncratic log-vol σ/√2, so every pair’s log-ratio still carries σrel = 2%/day and any common market factor cancels (it must — a ranking is scale-invariant). Then P(X largest) = ∫ φ(z) Πj≠X Φ([ln(capX/capj) + s·z]/s) dz with s = (σ/√2)√T, evaluated by 481-node Simpson quadrature on [−8, 8] in the browser on every refresh (≈1 ms). It agrees with a 2 000 000-path Monte Carlo of the same process to 0.05 pt, and its legs sum to 100 by construction rather than by subtraction. Second- and third-place fairs come from the same simulation and are re-baked each run; they are no longer the independence-assuming products this box used to warn about. T is in trading days (3 to Aug 31 / 24 to Sep 30 / 88 to Dec 31, counted from the Aug 27 UTC snapshot date; holidays Sep 7, Nov 26, Dec 25). The gap-vol rule adopted after the AMZN miss stands: any single-name leg with an earnings date inside its window gets a σ×2 sensitivity case (NVDA reported Aug 26 — the case fired and resolved bullish; Micron reports Sep 29, outside its ladder — the August MU ladder is priced on realised vol, not event vol). What is still wrong with this model. It assumes no persistent relative drift — precisely the assumption the market rejects — so treat “edge” as model-vs-market disagreement, not profit. It assumes zero correlation in the idiosyncratic shocks, which is right for ranks but wrong if the names de-correlate asymmetrically. A σ = 3%/day sensitivity case moves August’s NVIDIA fair from 99.18% to 95.75% and December’s from 70.82% to ≈57.3% — that band is wider than most of the edges now on the page, and it is the honest reason nothing here is sized above $350. The parameter this model does not pin down — read before sizing anything. The published σ = 2%/day was only ever calibrated on the four leader-vs-challenger pairs, because that is all the old formula used. The exact-rank integral needs all ten pairs, and the six challenger-vs-challenger vols are free. Holding the leader pairs at exactly 2.0%/day and sweeping the challenger-challenger vol across its admissible range moves the answer more than the σ sensitivity does: on the Aug 18 caps December NVIDIA ran roughly 61.0–86.4 across 1.3–2.8%/day — a ~25-point band that brackets the 72.5 market. The sweep has NOT been re-run on the Aug 20 caps — and this walk sharpened the point in a new way: with the caps frozen and the tape shut, the clock alone moved every fair on the page (the December leader 69.7 → 70.82, the September 2nd seat 71.8 → 72.67, sep2NVDA 10.05 → 9.66 — enough to retire a card outright). A parameter band wider than the edges is one problem; a fair that drifts a point per calendar day is another, and both argue the same way about sizing. The sweep’s value as a filter was demonstrated overnight: NVDA-3rd-September’s NO-fair spans 96.1–99.2 across it, and the NO — which traded 87–88, under the band’s floor — converged to 95 in one overnight session, unexecuted (retired row 67); the Alphabet-Sept-crown NO inherits the sweep-proof slot (fair band 95.8–100.0 vs a 97.9¢ NO cost tonight). The MSFT-3rd-Sept leg the account bought Aug 6 is the opposite case: its fair sweeps 1.3–15.1 around a 7.3¢ fill (mark 7.95 this morning, dead on the un-swept 7.7 fair), the widest relative band on the page, which is why it stays a punt and why its epilogue card retired on the Aug 20 evening walk (row 102). Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon co-move with each other more than any of them co-moves with NVIDIA, which argues the true challenger-challenger number is below 2%/day — i.e. the model as published is, if anything, too generous to the second-place trades and too harsh on the December leader. This is the single largest known uncertainty on the page and it is not in any of the numbers above. Small legs are now read off the books, not guessed. The untracked-competitor allowance was 1.25 (Aug) and 3.65 (Dec) with no stated source; the actual quotes are Tesla 0.15 + Aramco 0.25 + Broadcom 0.05 in August (0.45) and Tesla 0.15 + SpaceX 0.80 + Aramco 0.25 in December (1.20 — all re-read this walk off their own books, all unchanged; Tesla-December prints 0.15 and SpaceX-December 0.9). Correcting it moved every leader leg ≈0.6 pt and pushed two tickets under the actionability bar — a reminder that a parameter nobody checks is a parameter that is wrong. September is baked, not live. The 60-second loop now covers August, September and December; every September figure on this page is re-simulated by hand each run (T = 24 trading days this run, 8,000,000-path Monte Carlo for the rank-2/rank-3 fairs) and does not update between runs. Empirical odds-move stats use the rolling ~31-close prices-history window (21 per-run prints for the September book). Mid prices are not executable — every ticket is sized against a walked book. Odds and books are the Aug 28, 2026 22:47 UTC Friday POST-CLOSE walk; caps are the Aug 28 closes — the session that unwound the print (NVDA −4.58%, lead 19.41% → 12.12%) and re-fired the December re-entry on inputs four hours old (rows 104/105 remain the proof of why fresh caps matter; tonight is the first time the rule they wrote produced a ticket). July resolved NVIDIA and its block has been retired from this tab; on-chain settlement is still unobserved at this snapshot — the July books continue to return quotes. Nothing here is financial advice; prediction markets can resolve against you on oracle judgment alone.

Treasuries — If the 10-Year Prints 5.00%

The 10-year Treasury printed 4.80% on Sep 8 and 4.83% on Sep 9, 2026 — the 4.8% rung resolved YES on the Sep 8 print (the account had 653.67 shares and sold every one at 99.9¢ that afternoon), and the 5.0% rung repriced from 41 to 70.5 in a week. The 30-year is 5.28%, 3 bp under its 5.31 record of Aug 17. This bake answers one question: if the 10-year goes on to print 5.00% before Dec 31, which Polymarket books pay the most for the dollar? The method is a joint Monte Carlo — 1.2 million paths of the 10-year (half driftless, half a re-fitted AR(1)), the 30-year and 5-year as spreads on top of it, the Freddie Mac mortgage rate as a weekly spread, and the S&P, gold, oil and the dollar driven off the same rate shocks through betas measured on 2026’s daily data — conditioned on the paths that touch 5.00, then compared with 105 live books walked through the reader’s own Chrome on Sep 9 at 23:30–23:50 UTC (the autodata Action is still down; every price here is a CLOB touch, not a gamma print). Three findings. First, the crowd front-ran the scenario on the main rung and left the September rungs behind: the 5.0%-before-2027 book asks 72 for a claim a pure random walk prices at 58–66 (61.5 at the measured σ), the fitted AR(1) at 53 (a mean reversion that is itself insignificant, t(φ−1) = −0.8), the tab’s 50/50 mixture at 57 — only the 2026 trend persisting (+0.37 bp/day, t = 1.1) gets to 74–82, while the “10Y hits 4.94 / 4.97 / 5.00 in September” books ask 25 / 20 / 15 for claims worth 60 / 50 / 40 on the paths where 5.00 prints — and 41 / 31 / 23 even unconditionally, because those books carry $39–$266 of bids and nobody repriced them to the 4.83 close. Second, the mortgage pair is the deepest clean expression: “30Y mortgage ≤6.50% in 2026” NO at 48 is worth 80 conditionally (56 unconditionally — CHEAP on its own), and “≥7.00%” YES at 53 is worth 75 (44.6 — RICH on its own, a scenario leg only). Third, the Fed complex is the only deep book that repays the scenario — two-hikes-in-2026 at 24 and upper-bound-4.25%-before-2027 at 28.5 against inputs of 40 and 52 — a stated set, anchored on the measured 0.9-point-per-basis-point next-day response of the September-hike book to the 10-year and propagated through the complex’s own identities (three meetings left, so the buckets must sum and the meeting legs must add to the expected number of hikes; the market’s own complex fails that second identity). Bitcoin and Ether are not scenario bets at all (rate beta ≈ 0, t = −0.8 / −1.4); gold and the S&P upside are scenario losers; the held gold-$5,000 leg and the SPX-8,200 touch are the two positions the scenario hurts. Every unconditional fair on the tab is re-derived on the Sep 9 close; the Sep 2 card exhibit is kept below, marked superseded where the numbers moved. Fictitious research page — not financial advice.

#1 · THE SEPTEMBER LADDER · RV 1.6–2.7× “10Y hits 4.88 / 4.91 / 4.94 / 4.97 / 5.00 in September” — five thin books that never repriced to the 4.83 close: asks 49 / 36 / 25 / 20 / 15 against conditional fairs 81 / 71 / 60 / 50 / 40

Resolves
Treasury.gov “Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates”, 10 Yr column, any print Sep 3–30 at or above the strike. Same source and same rounding as the before-2027 ladder — a true 4.935 prints 4.94.
Where it is
4.83 on Sep 9. The strikes are 5 / 8 / 11 / 14 / 17 bp away with 15 SIFMA sessions left in the window (Sep 10–30).
Model, if 5.00 prints by Dec 31
P(4.88 in Sep) 81% · 4.91 71% · 4.94 60% · 4.97 50% · 5.00 40% · 5.10 12%. Across every model variant in the sensitivity table the 4.88 figure sits in 78–83, the 4.94 in 56–66, the 5.00 in 36–49 — these are the least model-dependent conditionals on the page.
Model, unconditional
66 / 53 / 41 / 31 / 23: the mids (42 / 27.5 / 22.5 / 16.5 / 14.5) are under the driftless fair on every rung. These are CHEAP without the scenario; the scenario doubles them.
Book
THIN, all five: $266 / $67 / $52 / $39 / $91 of bids; the offer sides under the conditional fairs total $415. This is a $300 idea, not a $3,000 one.
Reasoning

The before-2027 ladder is where the crowd went: its 5.0% rung traded 48.5 → 70.5 on Sep 9 (21 on Aug 31, 39.5 on Sep 1). The September ladder is the same event on a shorter clock, priced by nobody — the 4.94 book has 11 bid levels worth $52. Conditional on the 10-year printing 5.00 at some point before Dec 31, the path has to pass through every strike below it; the only question the September books ask is when. In the joint simulation 40% of the 5.00-paths print it inside September (median first print 10/07), and even the paths that print 5.00 in October or later have printed 4.88 in September 68% of the time (4.91: 51%, 4.94: 34%) — a third of the late paths do spend the whole of September under 4.88, which is what the 4.88 leg’s 19-point discount to certainty is for.

The unconditional numbers matter too, because the ticket is not a pure scenario bet: at σ = 4.3 bp/day a driftless 10-year prints 4.94 inside 15 sessions 41% of the time and the book asks 25. If the scenario fails — the yield rolls over from here — the September rungs lose together with the 5.0% position; if it succeeds they pay 2–3× while the 5.0% rung pays 1.4×. That asymmetry is the whole reason to own the shorter ladder alongside (or instead of adding to) the long one.

What can go wrong: a print of 4.87 on Sep 30 pays nothing on any of these; the “in September” window is 15 sessions and the rounding rule is the friend of the YES holder by half a basis point only. And the asks quoted here are single small levels — a $40 order can move them.

Optional lottery: 5.10 in September ≤4.6¢ (4.2 × 40, 4.3 × 631, 4.6 × 50 — $31), worth 12 on the scenario and 6.7 without it.

Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, the weekly 30-year fixed print (Thursdays), any week ending on or before Dec 31. 6.71 on Sep 3; 17 prints left, the first on Sep 10 (Freddie publishes on Wed Nov 25 in Thanksgiving week).
The link to the 10-year
PMMS = 10Y + spread. The spread was 1.92 on the Sep 3 print (6.71 − 4.79, the prior session’s print); the model runs it as a weekly AR toward 1.97 with 4 bp of noise, read off the prior session’s 10-year print (the Sep 10 print rides the known 4.83). 6.50 needs the 10-year near 4.53; 7.00 needs it near 5.03.
Model, if 5.00 prints
P(PMMS ≤ 6.50 by Dec 31) = 20% → NO worth 80 · P(PMMS ≥ 7.00) = 75% · P(≥ 7.25) = 23%. The 5.00-paths average 4.955 on Dec 31 and spend most of the quarter above 4.80; a 6.50 PMMS print on one of them needs a 30-bp round trip inside the window.
Model, unconditional
≤6.50: 44% (NO worth 56 vs 48 — CHEAP on its own) · ≥7.00: 45% vs a 50 mid — RICH on its own (+5.4 on the ±2.5 band): a scenario leg, not a value leg. The 6.75 rung (97.9 mid) is priced as already done: the Sep 10 print off a 4.80–4.83 ten-year lands 6.74–6.77.
Book
6.50 LOW: 52 × 25 / 55 × 65 — 697 shares of NO available at ≤52 ($349). 7.00 HIGH: 47 × 270 / 53 × 303 — 323 sh at ≤61 ($173). OK / THIN.
Reasoning

The two mortgage books disagree with each other and with the ladder. The 6.50-LOW book at a 53.5 mid says a 6.50 print is a coin-flip; the 5.0%-before-2027 book at 70.5 says the ten-year is more likely than not to go 17 bp higher. Both cannot be right in a world where the mortgage rate is the ten-year plus two points, and the second book is the deep one. Conditioning on the ladder’s own scenario settles it: on the paths that print 5.00, the PMMS gets to 6.50 one time in five.

The spread is the risk. Since Aug 6 the PMMS has run 1.92–2.06 over the prior session’s 10-year (mean 1.99 — the model’s 1.97 is a touch conservative for both legs). If the spread’s mean fell to 1.80 (where it sat in the 2025 easing) the NO is worth ≈61 on the scenario; if it dropped to 1.80 at once, ≈48 — the edge on this leg is the spread staying where it has been, and the reader should size it as a spread bet as much as a rates bet. If the spread widened (mortgage stress), the 7.00 leg pays sooner. The pair is long the spread on one leg and short it on the other, which is the point of running both.

The 7.00 leg is the weaker half: it is RICH unconditionally (45 vs 50) and its book is thin (6 bid levels, $130). It belongs in the basket as a scenario bet only; the 6.50-NO leg belongs there on either view.

THE TICKET: Buy NO on 6.50-LOW at ≤52¢ (equivalently sell YES into the 52 × 25, 51 × 316, 50 × 100, 49 × 47, 48 × 209 bids — NO at 48 × 25, 49 × 316, 50 × 100, 51 × 47, 52 × 209): 697 sh, $349 — sized to $200 in the basket. #4 · FED: THE SECOND HIKE · RV 1.6–1.8× · INPUT-DRIVEN “Exactly 2 Fed hikes in 2026” at 24 · “Fed upper bound reaches 4.25%+ before 2027” at 28.5 · “upper bound 4.25% at end-2026” at 25.3 — against scenario inputs of 40 / 52 / 40, unconditional mids 23 / 27.6 / 23.2

federalreserve.gov — the target range after each FOMC (Sep 15–16, Oct 27–28, Dec 8–9); the upper bound is 3.75% today, so 4.25% is two 25-bp hikes.
Why an input, not a model
A scheduled vote is not a diffusion. The tab does not simulate the FOMC; it states a conditional set (table below) and anchors it on one measured number: over Aug 1 – Sep 9 the Sep-hike book moved +0.90 points per basis point of the 10-year (next-day, corr 0.62, n = 26) and any-hike-2026 +0.53. A 17-bp move to 5.00 maps to ≈ +15 on the Sep-hike book and ≈ +9 on any-hike; the inputs shade both (Sep 64, any 86 — the slope is fragile: drop the single largest day, Aug 29, and it is 0.69) and derive everything else from the identities. Three meetings are left, so the buckets are 0/1/2/3 = 14/34/40/12 and the meeting legs must add to the expected count: Sep 64 + Oct 38 + Dec 46 = 1.48 hikes ≈ 0.34 + 0.80 + 0.36 = 1.50. Upper bound ≥ 4.25 before 2027 = 2 + 3 = 52; ≥ 4.50 = 12; by-Oct 76; no cuts 97.5.
Scenario value
2 hikes: 40 vs 24 ask (1.67×). ≥ 4.25 before 2027: 52 vs 28.5 (1.82×). End-2026 at 4.25: 40 vs 25.3 (1.58×). The three are the same claim in three wrappers; the first is the deep one.

2-hikes: 22 × 9,171 / 24 × 135, $101,353 of offers — DEEP; 1,964 sh at ≤26 ($496). ≥4.25: 26.6 × 14 / 28.5 × 20, 297 sh at ≤30.4 ($88) — OK. End-4.25: 21.1 × 5 / 25.3 × 10 — thin above 25.3.
Coherence check
Unconditional, the market’s own complex: 0/1/2/3 = 25.5/49.5/23/4.5 (sums 102.5), any-hike 73.5, ≥4.25-before-2027 27.5 ≈ 2+ hikes 27.5 — but its meeting legs (53.5 + 30.5 + 43.5 = 1.28 expected hikes) do not match its buckets (0.495 + 0.46 + 0.14 = 1.09): the market prices the meetings hotter than the count. The scenario set is built so that both identities hold, which is part of why the two-hikes bucket moves most.
Reasoning

The ten-year does not go to 5.00 in a vacuum. In 2026 the long end has sold off on oil (the Iran war) and on the Fed re-pricing from cuts to hikes; on the days the ten-year rose, the September-hike book rose the next day almost point for point per basis point. If the yield prints 5.00 the FOMC that meets six days after this bake is more likely to hike, the October meeting more likely to follow, and the “exactly two hikes” bucket — the market’s second-choice outcome at 23 — becomes the modal one.

Two hikes is the shape of the claim that pays best, because the market has spread its probability across one hike (49.5) and no hike (25.5) and left the second hike at 23. The scenario moves mass from “none” and “one” to “two” and “three” (the input set: 14/34/40/12); the ≥4.25-before-2027 book is the union of two-and-three and is the same bet with the three-hike tail thrown in for four extra points.

What the tab cannot claim: that the 0.9-pt/bp slope survives a 17-bp move (it is a local, next-day response measured over six weeks), or that a 5.00 print caused by a supply or term-premium shock — rather than an inflation shock — would move the FOMC at all. The inputs are stated so they can be argued with; every row of the conditional table that rests on them says INPUT.

THE TICKET: Exactly-2-hikes YES at ≤26¢: 24 × 135, 25 × 1,176, 26 × 653 — 1,964 sh, $496 available; the basket takes 300 sh ($72). ≥4.25-before-2027 YES at ≤30.4¢: 28.5 × 20, 29.1 × 80, 29.6 × 57, 30.4 × 140 — 297 sh, $88. Skip the end-2026 bucket (same claim, thinner, and it also needs no cut after the hikes).
Value rank #4 · the deepest scenario expression on the page; input-driven — read the Fed input table before sizing.

#5 · THE 5.0% RUNG ITSELF · RV 1.4× ON THE SCENARIO · RICH WITHOUT IT “10Y hits 5.0% before 2027” at 72 — the direct claim pays 100 on the scenario (1.39×), but a pure random walk prices it at 61.5 and the fitted AR(1) at 52.7 (57.1 mixture) against a 70.5 mid: HOLD the 10,983.63 shares, do not add, and know that the bid side is $1,574

Idea added Sep 10, 2026View on Polymarket ↗
Resolves
Treasury.gov 10 Yr par print ≥ 5.00 by Dec 31. Barrier 17 bp (16.5 effective). T = 77 SIFMA sessions.
Model
Martingale σ 4.3: 61.5 · σ 3.8 (the 20-day realised): 57.6 · σ 5.0: 66.0 · AR(1) as fitted (attractor 4.705): 52.7 · AR(1) with no pull: 63.0 · random walk + 2026’s +0.37 bp/day drift: 82.3 · +0.20 bp/day: 73.6. Mixture 57.1.
Market
69 × 120 / 72 × 245, mid 70.5. On the daily tape: 21 (Aug 31) → 39.5 (Sep 1) → 55.5 (Sep 3) → 29.5 (Sep 6) → 48.5 (Sep 8) → 70.5 (Sep 9). RICH by 13.4 on the mixture, FAIR only against the drift case.
Held
10,983.63 sh at 23.15¢, marked $7,743 (+$5,200). The whole bid side of the book is $1,574 across 31 levels, 69 × 120 at the touch — roughly a quarter of the position has a bid at any price.
If it prints
the position becomes $10,983.63 — $3,240 more than the mark; if the yield rolls over, the mark evaporates through a bid side that cannot absorb a tenth of it.
Reasoning

The Sep 2 bake called this rung CHEAP at 41 against 47.3 and said the fill history was a mark, not a value. Both halves aged well and badly at once: the yield went to 4.83 and the mid went to 70.5, so the model moved 10 points and the market moved 30. What the market is now paying for is a continuation of 2026’s drift — +0.37 bp/day since January, which over 77 sessions is 28 bp and would carry the yield through 5.00 on its own. The t-statistic on that drift is 1.15. The tab does not price on it and does not pretend it is impossible — and it is fair to the other side too: the AR(1)’s pull toward 4.70 has t(φ−1) = −0.8, is a fit to a series that went 4.19 → 4.83 (half-sample attractors 4.29 and 4.67), and at 4.83 amounts to −0.16 bp/day. Neither drift is established; the mixture straddles them and the pure walk (61.5) is the honest centre. RICH by 13 on the mixture, by 9 against the walk; FAIR only against the trend.

This is why the direct rung ranks fifth on a page about its own scenario. Every dollar spent here at 72 returns $1.39 if 5.00 prints; the same dollar in the September 4.94 book returns $2.41 and in the two-hikes book $1.46, and both of those are cheap or fair without the scenario while this one is rich without it. The rung is the right thing to own if you already own it; it is the wrong thing to buy more of at 72.

The unsellable-mark argument from Sep 2 is stronger, not weaker, at 70.5: the book is 31 bid levels and $1,574 for a $7,743 position. A trim would have to be worked at 69/68 for ~280 shares before the price is 58. There is no exit here; there is only the print or its absence.

THE TICKET: HOLD. No add at 72. If the reader must add scenario exposure, the order of preference is the September ladder (#1), the mortgage pair (#2), the 5.2% rung (#3), then the Fed second hike (#4), and only then this book — and only under 57¢. No trim either: the 69 × 120 / 68 × 162 bids are the exit for 282 shares of 10,983.
Value rank #5 · the largest position and the thinnest exit on the tab.

Where the curve is
30Y 5.28, 10s30s +45 bp — the tightest of 2026 (range 44–68, mean 56; the AR fit’s attractor 54.5). 5Y 4.61, 5s10s +22 bp (24 → 22 over the six September prints).
Model
The 30Y spread is an AR(1) on 2026 data (φ 0.964, mean 54 bp, β to Δ10Y -0.19, residual 1.5 bp/day). On a 5.00 ten-year the 30-year is 5.45 at today’s spread and 5.54 at the mean; 5.40 prints on 99.8% of the scenario paths and 77% of all paths — at the 2026-fitted spread beta (−0.19 bp per bp). Over Aug 27 – Sep 9 the local beta was −0.44 (the 10Y rose 16 bp, the spread fell 7); at that rate a 5.00 print gives a 5.375 thirty-year and the conditional is nearer 90 than 99. The 5Y spread is the weakest piece of the model — six prints and an assumed 0.97 persistence — so the 4.78 conditional (37) carries a ±10-point haircut.
Book
30Y 5.40: 71 × 121 / 77 × 60, $193 of offers — 80 sh at ≤78 ($62), THIN. 5Y 4.78: 28 × 192 / 29 × 323, 856 sh at ≤30 ($254), THIN.
Reasoning

The 30-year leg is the near-certain companion of the scenario — a 5.00 ten-year with the 2026 range of the 10s30s spread is a 5.44–5.68 thirty-year — and the book prices it at 74 because it also has to be bought without the scenario, where it is worth 77. That makes it fair on its own and a 1.3× on the scenario, with the whole payoff coming from the tail where the ten-year goes to 5.00 and the long bond does not follow (the spread has never been under 44 bp this year; it would need 40).

“5Y hits 4.78 in September” is the cheapest curve leg on the scenario and the least trustworthy: it needs a 17-bp move in the five-year inside 15 sessions, and it needs the 5s10s spread to hold at 22 while the ten-year rallies to 5.00 — in a bear-steepening (Fed on hold, term premium up) the five-year lags and this book loses even when the ten-year prints. It pays best if the move is a Fed re-pricing; it is a hike bet wearing a curve costume.

Neither leg belongs in the basket’s first $1,000; both are where the next $300 goes.

The timing problem
the September book resolves Sep 16; only 8% of the scenario paths have printed 5.00 by then (40% by Sep 30, 72% by the Oct 28 meeting). Buying Sep-hike YES is a bet that the FOMC sees what the bond market is pricing, not that the print has happened.
The kill-switch (Sep 2 rule)
this book governs the ladder’s add rule — RE-ARMED at ≥45¢ on three consecutive walks on Sep 2; still armed at 53.5 (over 45 on every daily print since Aug 29 except Sep 4’s 42.5). That rule said do not add to the 5.0% rung while this book is over 45; the account added 1,593 shares anyway on Aug 31 – Sep 1 and the rung went to 70. The rule was wrong about the direction and right about the risk.
Reasoning

If a reader wants the scenario in thousands of dollars rather than hundreds, this is the only place on Polymarket it can be bought. The multiples are small because these books are efficient — 54 × 29,647 is a real market — and the tab’s inputs move them by 3–11 points, not by 30. The October meeting book is the best of the four on the numbers (30.5 → 38, 1.23×) and the least talked about: the market has the October hike as a 30% event standing alone and a 66% event cumulatively, which is coherent, and the scenario lifts the standalone number most.

The reason to prefer these over the direct rung at 72 is not the multiple, it is the correlation structure: the rung pays only if the print happens; the hike books pay if the FOMC acts on the same information that would produce the print, whether or not the print itself arrives by Dec 31. On the paths where the yield gets to 4.95 and stalls, the rung pays nothing and the hike books pay most of what they would have.

What they are not: value bets. Every one is priced inside a point or two of the tab’s unconditional input (which is the market itself); the tab has no independent model of the FOMC and says so.

THE TICKET: Oct-hike YES at ≤31¢ (the best of the four; 10,692 sh at the touch); Sep-hike YES at ≤54¢ for a reader who wants it settled in six days. Idea added Sep 10, 2026View on Polymarket ↗
Method — the lift, not the model
For markets that do not resolve on Treasury.gov the tab does not trust its own unconditional number (a lognormal cannot price a crash strike). It takes the market mid as the unconditional truth and multiplies by the model’s lift = P(event | 5.00 prints) ÷ P(event), which depends on the measured beta, the scenario’s rate path — and the volatility the diffusion runs at: the S&P runs at the 22.8% its own 6,200 rung implies, not the 13% realised, because at 13% a −19% barrier is a five-sigma event whose lift is a number about nothing (it printed 1.5× before this was fixed; it is 1.23× now). Lift on oil-ATH 1.43, WTI-110 1.28, SPY-730 1.12, SPY-740 1.09.
The betas (2026 daily log returns on Δ10Y per 10 bp)
WTI +3.63% (t +5.7, R² 16%) · S&P -0.95% (t -6.2, R² 24%) · gold -0.82% (t -2.3) · Bitcoin -0.38% (t -0.8) · Ether -0.92% (t -1.4). Oil is the strong one — and the causality runs the other way: 2026’s rate shocks were oil shocks (corr 0.40; Δ10Y ≈ 0.45 bp per 1% oil).
What the scenario does to each
On the 5.00-paths the S&P ends the year 40% likely to be 5% lower vs 36% unconditionally; gold 41% vs 37%; oil’s September touches lift by 10–28%; the dollar-100 touch by 14% (assumed β +0.30, not measured — DXY is not on Hyperliquid).
Book
Oil-ATH: 11 × 18,151 / 12 × 1,521, $236,497 of offers — DEEP. WTI-110: 17 × 487 / 20 × 3,938 — DEEP. SPY-730: 19 × 5 / 20 × 5, 540 sh at ≤21. SPY-740: 32 × 236 / 35 × 165. CPI-4.5: 10 × 5,542 / 11 × 2,620, $2,714 of offers.
Reasoning

The oil-ATH book is the scenario’s most likely cause priced as its consequence: WTI needs $147.27 (a 52% rally from 97) and the market gives it 11.5. Conditioning on a 5.00 ten-year lifts it 43% through the beta — but the beta is oil driving rates, not rates driving oil, so the honest reading is “the paths on which the ten-year prints 5.00 are disproportionately the paths on which oil has spiked.” That is true and the book is deep; it is also the one row on this page where a reader who thinks the next 17 bp come from the Fed rather than from Brent should ignore the lift entirely.

SPY-730 in September is the equity leg: a −4.2% touch inside 15 sessions, priced 19.5 by the market and lifted to 22 by the scenario (the S&P’s beta is −0.95% per 10 bp, t −6.2 — the most significant rate beta on the page). It is the cheapest way to own “rates up, stocks down” here, and it is only a LEAN (1.09× at the ask); the December SPX-6,200 touch the account holds (65.56 sh) lifts 1.23× at the market’s own implied vol, where the model’s unconditional 9.2 sits next to the 10.1 mid.

CPI-above-4.5 is an input (10.5 → 13.5): a 5.00 print that comes from oil is an inflation print in the making; one that comes from term premium is not. Lift 1.29, deep book, small edge.

Sides: the table picks whichever side has the higher conditional RV; a row where both sides are under 1.0× shows the less-bad one and a NEUTRAL badge. SCENARIO BUY = RV ≥ 1.35 with at least $20 offered under the conditional fair; LEAN = RV ≥ 1.15. Thin books (THIN / NO MARKET) are flagged, not excluded — the September ladder is thin and is still the best value on the page, at its own size. Every P on a MODEL row is a simulation frequency on 1.2 million paths (standard error ≤ 0.1 pt); every LIFT-row fair is the market’s mid times a model ratio, so it inherits whatever the market got wrong unconditionally.

Anchor: over Aug 1 – Sep 9 the Sep-hike book moved +0.90 pts per bp of the 10-year on the next day (corr 0.62, n 26) and the any-hike-2026 book +0.53 (corr 0.47); same-day correlations are ≈0 because the daily price points sit at 00:00 UTC, before the Treasury print. A 17-bp move maps to ≈+15 / +9; the slope is fragile (drop Aug 29, the largest day, and it is 0.69; drop the three largest, 0.57), so the Sep and any-hike inputs are shaded to 64 and 86 and everything else is propagated through the identities: three meetings left, so 0/1/2/3 hikes = 14/34/40/12 (sum 100); expected hikes from the meetings 0.64 + 0.38 + 0.46 = 1.48 ≈ from the buckets 0.34 + 0.80 + 0.36 = 1.50; ≥4.25 before 2027 = 2 + 3 = 52; ≥4.50 = 3 = 12; end-2026 buckets 14/34/40/12; by-Oct 76 ≤ any 86; Sep 64 ≤ by-Oct. The market’s own complex satisfies the first identity and fails the second (meetings 1.28 vs buckets 1.09). These are inputs; the table marks every row that uses them INPUT.

Bitcoin and Ether are set to β = 0 (t −0.8 / −1.4): the point estimates are negative and insignificant, and the tab does not run a channel it cannot defend. Oil’s β is the reverse channel — Δ10Y regressed on oil returns gives +0.45 bp per 1% (t 5.7, corr 0.40) — so oil rows are “paths where rates rise are paths where oil rose”, not a forecast that a rate move lifts oil. The S&P beta (−0.95%/10 bp, t −6.2) is the only one strong enough to move a December price much; gold’s (−0.82, t −2.3) is enough to make the held $5,000 leg a scenario loser. Vols used in the simulation are round numbers between the full-year and 60-day realised figures; the SPX vol (13%) is below the tail the market prices, which is why SPX rows use the lift, not the model.

The conditionals are what the page trades on, and most of them barely move: 4.88-in-September given 5.00 is 78–83 everywhere, 4.94 is 56–66, 5.00-in-September 36–49. The two that move are the 5.20 and 5.50 rungs (17–69 and 0.2–27), because whether the yield keeps going after it touches 5.00 is exactly the question the AR(1) and the random walk answer differently — which is why the 5.2% rung is ranked #3 and called a scenario bet, and the 5.5% rung is not ranked at all. 300,000 paths per variant; standard errors ≤ 0.1 pt on P(5.00), ≤ 0.2 on the conditionals. #1 · ONE BASIS POINT RUNG 0 · 4.79 vs 4.80 The 10-year closed 4.79% — the year’s high, one bp under the 4.8% rung’s barrier — and the rung quotes 92 × 79 / 98 × 174 with $2,282 of bids under it: the first rung on this ladder that has ever been sellable in size SEP 10: RESOLVED — the 4.80 print came Sep 8; the account sold 653.67 sh at 99.9¢ that afternoon (row 297). This card is history.

Idea added Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

The Treasury.gov par curve printed 4.79% on Sep 1 — above the Jul 31 and Aug 31 prints of 4.75, the highest 10 Yr value in the 168 sessions of the 2026 file, and one basis point under the value that resolves this rung YES. The market moved with it: rung 0 went 77.5 → 85.5 → 88.5 → 76.0 (15:00Z) → 90.0 → 95.0 through the session on the 3-hour tape, and the walk finds it at 92 × 79 / 98 × 174 — a 6-point spread, but a bid side of 35 levels and $2,282 (90 × 1,044 is the wall) against a position of 448.86 shares. The model is nearly indifferent: martingale 93.0, AR(1) 92.4, mixture 92.7 — both legs simulated on daily prints rounded to two decimals, because a true 4.795 prints 4.80 and pays, so the effective barrier is half a basis point: 93 driftless paths in 100 produce at least one 4.80 print inside 82 sessions, and the 7 that do not are the paths on which the yield falls from here and never comes back. At 95 the mid is 2.3 points over — FAIR at the ±2.5 band, and the least interesting number on the tab: the difference between 93 and 95 is one up-day of one basis point.

What the account did with it is the story. Since Aug 31 the rung has been traded eight times: bought 70.25 at 82.57¢ (Aug 31 15:56Z), 120.58 at 82.93¢ (Sep 1 01:10Z — ledger row 257), 20.90 at 90.91¢ (03:56Z), 10 + 10 at 82/81¢ (08:28Z); then SOLD 253.27 at 99¢ (12:10Z) while the 3-hour mid was 84.5 — the ladder’s best single exit ever, $250.74 into an air pocket — then bought 110.05 back at 90.87¢ (17:29Z) and 41.65 at 96.04¢ (Sep 2 00:22Z). Net: 509.53 → 448.86 shares at an 80.15¢ blended basis (the data-api’s own figure), the position marking $426.42 and walking out for $406.10 at a 90.47¢ VWAP over three levels. Ledger row 257 recorded the position as 439.28 shares at a 71.43¢ blend; it was 509.53 — the Aug 31 buy had not been ingested. Corrected in rows 258–271.

THE TICKET: Hold. No order. There is nothing to buy under fair (the 92 bid sits under the 92.7 mixture) and nothing to sell over it that the 99¢ sale did not already sell better. If the rung prints, 448.86 shares become $448.86; if the yield falls, the 90 × 1,044 wall is the exit and it is real. The one instruction: do not buy the 98 offer — it is 6 points over the mixture for a claim whose upside is capped at $1.00, and the 96.04¢ fill at 00:22Z already did.

Idea added Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

Aug 10 withdrew the “largest edge on leadsure.com” because the mixture (35.0) sat on top of the market (34.0). Tonight the same mixture, re-run on the Sep 1 close, prints 47.3 against a 41.0 mid — CHEAP by 6.3, RV 1.15×. Nothing about the model changed in the market’s favour: the AR(1) re-fit is slightly more mean-reverting than before (φ 0.98476, attractor 4.632%, half-life 45 trading days — the attractor rose 8 bp with the data), σ measured 4.21–4.31 bp/day across every window, and sixteen sessions came off the clock. What changed is spot: 4.72 → 4.79, a 21-bp barrier that a two-decimal print makes 20.5, and a driftless random walk crosses it in 82 sessions 55.5% of the time. The AR(1) says 39.1. Half of each is 47.3.

Now the book. The rung round-tripped 42 → 28 → 41 inside Sep 1 on the 3-hour tape (28 at 15:00Z and 18:00Z — the account bought 39.99 shares at 38¢ at 04:01Z, on the way down), and at the walk it is 33 × 75 bid / 49 × 14 offered: a 16-point canyon with $532 of bids on 16 levels beneath it. The position is 10,983.63 shares at a 23.15¢ basis (data-api), marking $4,503.29 and walking out for $532.00 at an 18.69¢ VWAP with 8,137.7 shares — 74% — bidless at any price. The Aug 10 falsification clause (1) said: if this bid side does not carry $1,000 within two weeks, the +$1,015 gain was never a gain and the tab says so permanently. It never carried $1,000 — $178 → $460 → $370 → $532 is the whole history — so, permanently: the 5.0% rung’s mark has never been a value. And the offer side is the reason the CHEAP badge earns no rank: the first ask is 49, 1.7 points over fair; capturable dollars under 47.3 are zero.

THE TICKET: No adds — the rule, restated against a CHEAP badge on purpose. A row can be cheap and untradeable at once; this one is. The resting-offer ticket (Trades #1) moves up into the canyon: 48¢ and 49¢, over the 47.3 fair and at or under the market’s only real ask. The account bought 1,593.34 shares of this rung between Aug 31 15:56Z and Sep 1 04:01Z at 27.88 / 29.89 / 38¢ — ingested tonight as rows 259, 260 and 265 — through a do-not-add that has now been violated eleven times. #3 · THE BEST RV ON THE TAB RUNG 2 · 17.4 vs 9.4 · 1.85× · $112 OF BIDS The 5.2% rung is priced at less implied vol than the 5.0% rung (2.78 vs 2.98 bp/day at the mids — a dent, though the two rungs’ touch-price bands overlap) — and the mixture says 17.4 against 9.4; the capturable edge is $5.06 on 147 shares SEP 10: SUPERSEDED — 25.65 against 22.3: RICH unconditionally, 39 on the 5.00-paths. See conditional book #3.

Idea added Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

Rung 2 quotes 5.9 × 30 / 12.9 × 9, mid 9.4, and has done nothing all week (9.3–10.1 on the 3-hour tape). The fresh mixture prints 17.4 — martingale 27.0 for a 40.5-bp effective barrier, AR(1) 7.8 — so the row is CHEAP by 8.0 and its RV, 1.85×, is the highest unconditional multiple on the Treasuries tab and the best unconditional line on the site’s Leaderboard (#32). Invert it and the reason shows: the mid implies 2.78 bp/day of volatility, LESS than the 2.98 the 5.0% rung implies one strike below it. The Aug 10 smile ran 1.94 / 3.11 / 3.38 / 4.48 / 4.97 / 5.87 — monotone. Tonight’s runs 2.98 / 2.78 / 4.85 / 5.13 / 6.49: a dent at the second rung, then the far strikes priced at 5–6.5 bp/day against a measured 4.3. The honest size of the dent: at touch prices the 5.0% rung implies 2.55–3.70 and the 5.2% rung 2.48–3.11 — the bands overlap, so this is a mid-to-mid observation on a 16-point canyon, not a measurement. Either the 5.2% rung is cheap relative to its neighbour, or the 5.0% rung is rich relative to it; the mixture says the former, the book says nobody is trading either.

The book, as always, is the verdict on the verdict: the bid side is $112 on 12 levels (5.9 × 30, 5.8 × 1,000 is the wall, then 5.5 × 200), the offer side is $18,874 stacked from 12.9 up, and the shares offered under the 17.4 fair total 147 shares for $5.06 of capturable edge. The position is 3,468.23 shares at an 8.89¢ basis, marking $326.01 and walking out for $91.34 at 2.63¢. RV 1.85× on a book that can absorb $20 of buying under fair is a number to publish, not a ticket to size.

THE TICKET: Buy ≤14.6¢, cap $21 (≈147 sh — the whole under-fair stack, $20.49). Standalone, and the smallest ticket on the tab by design. Resolution — Who Decides These Markets, and Where It Can Go Wrong

Ideas as of Aug 10, 2026 · re-checked Sep 2, 2026 00:55 UTC (Tuesday post-close walk) Four different definitions of “touch” across one tab — a daily par yield, an upper bound, a 1-minute candle, a futures settlement and a weekly survey · three of tonight’s tickets exist because of the resolution text, not despite it · the ladder card matters most tonight: the 4.8% rung resolves on the first daily par-yield print at or above 4.80, and Sep 1 printed 4.79 · read before sizing anything

THE LADDER — A DAILY PRINT, AND A WINDOW THAT OPENED IN 2025 The rule verbatim, and the 168 sessions that have already run against it — the highest of them is yesterday’s

Idea added Aug 10, 2026 · Reviewed Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

“This market will resolve to ‘Yes’ if the Treasury 10-year yield reaches or is higher than the listed value for any date between [Nov 11, 2025 and Dec 31, 2026]. … The resolution source for this market is the Department of the treasury, specially the data listed under ‘Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates’ for the column ‘10 Yr’.” Three consequences. First, the barrier is a published daily par yield, not an intraday tick — a session that trades through 4.80% and prints 4.79% pays nothing, which is precisely why the model simulates daily prints rounded to two decimals rather than a continuous path — and precisely what Sep 1 did. Second, the window has been running since Nov 11, 2025. Third, the record is checked against the file itself: of the 168 sessions of 2026, the highest 10 Yr print is 4.79% on Sep 1, 4.75% (Jul 31, Aug 31) is second, and zero sessions have reached 4.80%. Rungs 0 through 5 are all live. Rung 0 resolves on the first print at 4.80 or above — Treasury posts the file by ~19:30 UTC on each business day, so the earliest YES is the Sep 2 close.

THE FED BOOKS — AN UPPER BOUND, A ROUNDING RULE, AND “CREDIBLE REPORTING” AGAIN 12.5 bp rounds UP to 25 · emergency cuts count toward the cut total · the year book cannot resolve NO until after Dec 8–9

Idea added Aug 10, 2026 · Reviewed Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

Every Fed row on this tab resolves on “the upper bound of the target federal funds range”, never the effective rate and never a Fed-speak signal. The meeting books resolve to the change “versus the level it was prior to” that meeting, and carry a rounding rule worth knowing: “if the target federal funds rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded up to the nearest 25” — an unlikely 12.5 bp move resolves the 25-bp bracket, not the no-change one. The year book resolves YES if the upper bound rises “at any point between January 1, 2026 and the Fed’s [final] 2026 meeting”, primary source federalreserve.gov, “however a consensus of credible reporting may also be used” — the same soft clause that governs the largest-company books. And the cut-count book explicitly counts emergency cuts outside scheduled meetings toward the total and stays open to Dec 31, 11:59 PM ET to catch them, which is exactly why the no-cuts leg and the emergency leg can be read as one distribution in ticket #6 — and why the account’s 250 emergency-cut YES (row 262) is a bet that the no-cuts leg it also owns resolves NO.

THREE MARKETS, THREE INCOMPATIBLE DEFINITIONS OF “TOUCH” SPX = a 1-minute candle on Yahoo · gold = a CME Active Month settlement · mortgage = a weekly Freddie Mac survey

Idea added Aug 10, 2026 · Reviewed Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

The tab’s three touch ladders are quoted in the same column and monitored on three different clocks, which is the hidden reason their implied volatilities are not comparable. SPX resolves off “any 1-minute candle” high or low “as reflected in Yahoo Finance’s 1-minute interval data”, regular trading hours only — effectively continuous monitoring, and an instantaneous wick counts; the page’s continuous-path touch model slightly overstates even that. Gold resolves off “the official CME settlement price for the Active Month” contract, where the Active Month is the nearest delivery-cycle month (Feb/Apr/Jun/Aug/Oct/Dec) that is not the spot month, rolling on the First Position Date — so an intraday spike to $5,000 that settles at $4,960 pays nothing, and the contract being measured changes underneath the holder before Dec 31; tonight’s $4,369.80 spot is the Dec ’26 contract, and the model’s continuous path understates the settlement-only barrier’s difficulty. The mortgage row resolves off the weekly Freddie Mac PMMS — about 17 observations left in the year, the coarsest monitoring on the page. Same word, three instruments, and only one of them is near-continuous.

WHERE THE TAIL TICKETS CAN GO WRONG — REVISIONS, ADVANCE ESTIMATES, AND A SETTLEMENT THAT LANDS IN 2027 The recession leg may not resolve until the Q4 advance estimate, weeks after every other row on this tab has paid — which is why it is not in the basket

Idea added Aug 10, 2026 · Reviewed Sep 2, 2026View on Polymarket ↗

Four ways the short-tail basket in ticket #12 can be right about the world and still lose. One: the recession leg resolves on advance estimates and reaches back to Q2 2025 — a revision that turns an old quarter negative can trigger it, and it “will stay open until the Advance estimate of Q4 2026 is published”, which lands well after Dec 31; capital committed past the horizon, so the leg is excluded from the basket rather than capped. Two: the inflation leg freezes on the year-end release — “any revisions to previously released CPI figures will not be counted” after it — so a hot print later revised away still resolves YES, and ticket #8 is short exactly that asymmetry; the Jul and Aug prints, which this page has not re-read, are two of the four remaining chances. Three: the year-end state-of-the-economy book resolves on the year-end U-3 and CPI-U prints and defaults if they are not published by Jan 31, 2027, so a data-release disruption is a live settlement risk on a $13 book. Four: the ladder’s own source is a government web page that this site has watched go stale for eleven days once already — and that is the page that decides whether 4.79 becomes 4.80. Every one of these is a reason the tail carries are capped at $750 combined rather than sized to their apparent edge — and prediction markets can resolve against you on oracle judgment alone.

Four cards, re-checked tonight against the live market descriptions, and one of them is now the most important paragraph on the tab: the ladder resolves on a published daily par yield, the Sep 1 file says 4.79, and the 4.8% rung the account holds 448.86 shares of pays on the first print at or above 4.80 — which the market prices at 95 and the model at 92.7. The inflation card’s “greater than” plus one-decimal reading (effective barrier 4.6%) is the reason ticket #8 exists; the Fed card’s emergency-cut clause is the reason ticket #6 begins with a sale. Unchanged and worth repeating: these are not exchange-cleared instruments; resolution runs through published data and, on the Fed rows, through a “consensus of credible reporting” clause that has already misfired elsewhere on this site. The 10-year rungs monitor on daily closes, gold on CME settlements of a contract that rolls, SPX on 1-minute candles, mortgages on a weekly survey — four monitoring frequencies, one column of prices, and a comparison between them is only ever approximate. Methodology, Sources & Honesty Box

Sep 10 addendum — the conditional book

The question changed, the model grew. The Sep 2 tab priced each rung on its own; the Sep 10 tab prices every market jointly so that it can condition on one event — a Treasury.gov 10 Yr print ≥ 5.00 before Dec 31. The 10-year is simulated exactly as before (600,000 driftless paths at σ 4.3 and 600,000 AR(1) paths at the re-fit φ 0.9875 / attractor 4.705 / residual 4.25 bp; prints rounded to two decimals before every barrier test; 77 SIFMA sessions). On top of each path: the 30Y−10Y spread as a fitted AR(1) (φ 0.964, mean 54 bp, β -0.19 to the day’s 10Y change, residual 1.5 bp), the 10Y−5Y spread as an assumed AR (0.97 persistence toward 24 bp — six prints is not a fit, and the 5Y rows say so), the Freddie Mac PMMS as the prior session’s 10Y print plus a weekly AR spread (1.92 → 1.97, ±4 bp) on the 17 print dates (16 Thursdays plus Wed Nov 25; the Sep 10 print rides the known 4.83), and six assets as lognormal diffusions whose daily return carries β × (Δ10Y / 10 bp) plus idiosyncratic noise: S&P (β -0.95, 22.8% vol — the 6,200 rung’s implied, not the 13% realised, so that the lifts are ratios of numbers the diffusion can actually price; rungs where the model’s own unconditional probability is under 5% are not lifted at all), gold (-0.82, 24%), WTI (+3.63, 45%), Bitcoin (0, 45%), Ether (0, 70%), DXY (+0.30 assumed, 6%). Conditioning is by selection: keep the paths where the 10Y prints 5.00, count every event on them. The mixture conditions properly — a model that produces more 5.00-paths gets more weight in the conditional, which is why the driftless walk dominates the conditionals and the AR(1) dominates the unconditional far rungs. Three methods, labelled on every row: MODEL (Treasury.gov / Freddie-resolved — the simulation’s own number), LIFT (market mid × the simulation’s conditional-to-unconditional ratio — used where the tab’s lognormal is not credible unconditionally, i.e. every equity, gold, oil, dollar and crypto row), INPUT (Fed and macro — stated conditionals anchored on one measured slope: the Sep-hike book moved +0.90 pts per bp of the 10-year, next day, over Aug 1 – Sep 9). What the page does not know: whether the next 17 bp come from oil, the Fed or term premium (the Fed inputs assume the first two); whether the local 0.9-pt/bp slope survives a 17-bp move; what the Parcl index reads today; whether 2026’s +0.37 bp/day drift (t 1.15) is a regime or noise — the market’s 70.5 on the main rung says regime, the pure walk says 58–66 and the fitted AR(1) 53. Books walked Sep 9 23:30–23:50 UTC through the reader’s Chrome from the clob.polymarket.com origin (asset_id and timestamp checked on each); positions and fills from data-api at 23:3xZ; the curve from the Treasury.gov TextView page (Sep 1–9 rows) appended to the 2026 CSV; Freddie Mac PMMS via FRED (MORTGAGE30US, 6.71 on Sep 3); spots from CNBC (SPX 7,636.36 close, GC Dec 4,437.80, WTI Oct 97.12, DXY 98.817, BTC 78,200, ETH 2,465); daily closes for the betas from Hyperliquid’s candle API (BTC, ETH, xyz:CL, xyz:GOLD, xyz:SP500). No trades were placed; no order was cancelled; no credential was stored.

The touch model

P(30Y prints ≥6.00% on a daily close by Dec 31) uses the exact drifted first-passage probability — Φ((μT−a)/σ√T) + e^(2μa/σ²)·Φ((−a−μT)/σ√T) — with a Broadie–Glasserman–Kou barrier shift (+0.5826·σ√Δt) because the ladder resolves on one daily print, not the intraday path. That distinction is not pedantry: in Oct 2023 the 10-year famously “hit 5%” intraday (5.02%) while the daily par yield peaked at 4.98% — and on Sep 1, 2026 the 10-year printed 4.79 against a 4.80 barrier. Re-derived Sep 2 on the Sep 1 close: a = 72.5 bp effective (6.00 − 5.27 = 73, less the half-point a two-decimal print rounds away — a true 5.995 prints 6.00 and pays), T = 82 SIFMA trading days (Sep 2 – Dec 31 less Sep 7, Oct 12, Nov 11, Nov 26, Dec 25 — the bond calendar, because the barrier is a Treasury.gov print and Treasury does not publish on those days; Aug 10 used 101 on the equity calendar, three more than the bond calendar’s 98), σ = 4.0 bp/day (measured: 20d 4.15, 40d 3.97, 60d 3.93, full-2026 3.79 across 167 daily changes). With zero drift, P = 3.9% (1.9% at σ = 3.5, 6.5% at 4.5). With 2026’s realised +0.246 bp/day carried forward, P = 10.9% — the drift’s t-statistic is 0.84 again, so the martingale number leads and the trend case sits beside it. The number fell from 5.4% on a barrier 2 bp closer because sixteen sessions came off the clock: first-passage probability scales with σ√T, and √82 is 9% smaller than √98.

The two models, and the mixture

Martingale: zero-drift random walk on the 10-year, σ = 4.3 bp/day (measured 4.21–4.31 across the 20d / 40d / 60d / full-year windows — the tightest spread of estimates the series has produced), priced by a 1,000,000-path simulation of daily closes rounded to two decimals — exact discrete monitoring on the print the market actually resolves on (a true 4.795 prints 4.80), which puts the effective barrier half a basis point inside each strike. The closed-form first-passage formula with the Broadie–Glasserman–Kou shift agrees within 0.1 point on every rung except the 4.8% one, where a 1-bp barrier is outside the shift’s regime and it over-states the rung by 0.9 point; the simulation is the published number. AR(1): re-fitted tonight on the 168 closes of 2026: φ = 0.98476, attractor 4.632%, residual σ 4.30 bp, half-life 45 trading days (Aug 10: 0.98089 / 4.549% / 35.9) — the attractor rose 8 bp with the data and the reversion slowed; its rung probabilities are Monte Carlo over the same 82 sessions, on the same rounded prints. The fair is their equal-weight mixture, and the honest reason is unchanged: neither survives on its own. φ̂ has a standard error of 0.017 (t(φ − 1) = −0.90), so the series cannot be told from a random walk; the martingale, meanwhile, ignores that yields have looked mean-reverting to everyone pricing these books all year. Tonight the mixture and the market disagree on the near rungs for the first time since Jul 31 — 47.3 vs 41.0 on 5.0%, 17.4 vs 9.4 on 5.2% — and the tab’s claim is narrower than it was in July: the market is pricing the two live rungs at less than half the martingale’s probability on books with $532 and $112 of bids, and the mixture is a reason not to sell them, not a reason to buy more.

The smile, and what a constant σ does to it

Inverting each rung to the σ that makes its mid fair at zero drift (closed form on the half-point-adjusted barrier) gives 2.98 / 2.78 / 4.85 / 5.13 / 6.49 bp per day across the 5.0 → 6.0 strikes (the 4.8% rung, one basis point out, has no meaningful implied σ — the solver runs to its ceiling). Aug 10 was 1.94 / 3.11 / 3.38 / 4.48 / 4.97 / 5.87, monotone. The far end still rises, and against a rising smile any constant-σ model must call the far rungs rich — the tab said on Aug 10 that it would not report that pattern as a finding twice, and it does not: the RICH badges on 5.5 / 5.7 / 6.0 are the assumption looking at itself. The dent at 5.2% (2.78 under 2.98) is new and is a finding of the weakest kind: it holds at the mids and dissolves at the touches (5.0% implies 2.55–3.70 across its 33/49 spread, 5.2% 2.48–3.11 across 5.9/12.9 — the bands overlap), so it says the two near rungs are quoted inconsistently, not traded inconsistently. The SPX ladder’s smile is 25.8 / 27.7 / 34.7 at −18.8 / −24.0 / −31.9% and gold’s is 31.3 / 34.9 at +14.4 / +37.3% — both rising with distance from spot, which is what index puts and, now, gold calls are supposed to do; the Aug 10 gold inversion was a $4,100-spot artefact and the $270 rally repaired it.

Ladders that are not the 10-year — SPX, gold, housing

SPX and gold are priced at their own deepest rung’s implied volatility — deepest by the smaller side of the book, so a thin rung is always judged against a liquid one — using a driftless reflection-principle touch over the 121 calendar days from Sep 1 to Dec 31. The anchor is a choice and it moved tonight (SPX 5,800 → 6,200; gold stays at $6,000); Monitor #10 shows what the other choice would have printed. Spots: SPX 7,631.47 (Sep 1 close, CNBC .SPX, corroborated by SPY 761.78 −0.69% on stockanalysis.com), gold $4,369.80 (Dec ’26 COMEX, CNBC @GC.1 delayed print 20:49 ET Sep 1). Housing (Sep 30 median US home value) settles on the Parcl Labs US price-per-square-foot index × 2,000 — not Zillow — and is modelled normal around the last Parcl read ($211/sqft → $422,000, Aug 10) with σ = 1.0% over the original 51-day window and the index’s −2.1%/yr trailing drift; the spot has not been refreshed since Aug 10 and the page says so on every housing row. Every non-ladder row that has no diffusion behind it — the Fed complex, CPI, recession, stagflation, the emergency cut, the mortgage row — carries NO MODEL and blank model columns; its ticket, where there is one, is a resolution-text or book-depth argument.

Books, and how thin they are

Every executable quote was CLOB-verified (bid/ask/depth, asset_id matched, book timestamps 00:49–00:57 UTC) at 00:55 UTC Sep 2, fetched through the reader’s own Chrome from the clob.polymarket.com origin because the site’s autodata Action has produced nothing since Aug 31 19:23Z; gamma is used for market discovery only (the seven housing token ids) and never for a price. The depth numbers matter more than the prices. The 10-year ladder marks $5,465.91 and liquidates into its own bid stacks for $1,045.47 — 80.9% — with the 5.0% leg filling 2,846 of 10,983.63 shares at an 18.69¢ VWAP and 74% finding no bid at any price; only rung 0, one basis point from resolving, walks inside 10% of its mark. And the account’s own orders move these books: eight fills on rung 0 since Aug 31 into a one-level offer side, 1,593 shares of rung 1 bought into a 16-level $532 bid side, a 192-share gold buy four points over tonight’s touch. On books with 9, 14, 16 and 30 shares at the touch, every mid on this table is partly the account’s footprint.

What would falsify this tab

The September FOMC passing without a hike while the 30Y closes back under 5.00% kills the premise outright. The Aug 10 commitments, scored: (1) tripped — the 5.0% rung’s bid side never carried $1,000 ($178 → $460 → $370 → $532), so the +$1,015 mark of Aug 10 is recorded permanently as not a gain; (2) partly — the smile did not flatten, but its two near rungs crossed at the mids (2.98 / 2.78), which is neither the convergence that would have reinstated the constant-σ model nor the monotone shape that retired it; (3) not yet — the 10-year is 4.79, not 4.85–4.90, and rung 1 is 41, not 45. Tonight’s commitments — one test the tab can fail, two procedures it binds itself to: (4) the mixture says the 5.0% rung prints 47 times in 100 and the 5.2% rung 17 — one December is one draw, so the score is cumulative: every near-rung call at ≥40% this ladder has made is logged, and if fewer than a third of them have printed after two full years of the ladder, the martingale leg is over-weighted; (5) a market price is not an outcome, so the old (5) is dropped — replaced by: if the 10-year closes ≥4.90 and the 5.0% rung still quotes under 46, the tab re-fits the AR(1) attractor on the new data and publishes whether the mixture moved, rather than moving the weight by hand; (6) if the $6,000 gold rung re-prices above 14 with spot inside ±2%, the ladder’s anchor is following one deep book rather than the ladder — the $5,000 leg gets priced at its own implied vol that walk, and the two numbers are shown side by side. Oil — If Brent Prints $130 by Oct 1

Brent settled $109.29 on Sep 10, 2026 (Nov ’26, +7.98% on the day; ICE high 109.68 — the Hyperliquid perp, which runs 3–4% under ICE, printed a 112.19 high) after Houthi strikes on Saudi energy facilities, a reported 1.9 mb/d fall in Saudi August output and a US–Iran exchange of strikes on tankers and warships; WTI (Oct ’26) settled 103.93, the 10-year printed 4.95% (+12 bp), the S&P closed −0.58%, gold −1.0%, the dollar +0.28%, Bitcoin −1.6%. This tab answers one question: if the front-month Brent contract trades $130 at any point by Oct 1 (+19% from here, 14 sessions), which Polymarket books pay the most for the dollar at today’s asks? The method is a joint bootstrap — 600,000 paths of Brent drawn from its own 2026 daily returns and intraday overshoots (two volatility regimes, 68% and 48% annualised, mixed 71/29 on the paths that touch), the CME active-month WTI as Brent minus a spread that rolls from the Oct to the Nov contract on Sep 18, the 10-year driven off oil at the measured +0.60 bp per 1% (t 6.7) plus its own noise, the 30-year and 5-year as spreads, and the S&P, gold, silver, the dollar and Bitcoin off the same oil shocks through 2026’s daily betas — conditioned on the 18.6% of paths that touch 130, then compared with 123 live books walked through the reader’s own Chrome on Sep 10 at 22:17 and 22:53 UTC (the autodata Action is down a twenty-first run; every price here is a CLOB touch, and the account’s own afternoon fills are in these books). Four findings. First, the WTI September ladder is the direct expression and it is mispriced by the roll: the $125 and $130 rungs ask 15.8 and 9.5 for claims worth 64 and 36 on the paths where Brent touches 130 — not 100, because from the Sep 18 session the market resolves on the November contract, which settled $9.78 under Brent tonight, and only 17% of the touches come before the roll. The held $120 rung (22.4 ask) is worth 97 on the scenario. Second, the deepest scenario books are the Iran ceasefire markets: a $130 print is, on this tab’s stated scenario weights, a Gulf-infrastructure war two times in five, a direct US–Iran escalation three in ten, an Israel–Iran collapse three in twenty — so “Israel × Iran ceasefire holds through Sep 30” NO at 16 is worth 38, “Iran full airspace closure by Sep 30” YES at 9 is worth 35, and there is $6,982 of NO resting under fair on the first and $3,252 of offers under fair on the second. Third, the cross-asset books price a $130 world as ordinary: SPY-touches-$720-in-September asks 19 for a claim worth 38 (the S&P beta to Brent is −0.15% per 1%, t −10.7 — a $130 tape takes the index to about 7,403), gold is a scenario loser (β −0.16, t −5.7 — the $4,100 September touch is worth 54 against a 39 ask) and the dollar a scenario winner (DXY 100.50 worth 54 against 31). Fourth, the rates books already priced it: the 10-year would print about 5.05 on Sep 30 under the scenario, but the 10Y-5.00-in-September book asks 82 for a claim worth 88 — the Treasuries tab’s September ladder was the trade of Sep 9, not Sep 10; the held 5.2% rung (worth 52 on the scenario at a 36 ask) is the one rates leg that still pays. The scenario itself is not cheap: the tab puts it at 18.6% (26.6 at the March-heavy vol, 10.7 at the recent vol); pushed back through the tab’s own roll mapping, the market’s WTI-$125 mid (15.7) implies about 24 — the market is near the high-vol regime’s 27, not between the two — and the $1,050 basket on card #10 returns about 0.8× if the tab’s 18.6 is right and breaks even at 28. The cards enumerate what rests on the books; the basket is the size. Fictitious research page — not financial advice.
