#1 · WTI $125 / $130 IN SEPTEMBER · RV 4.1× / 3.8× “WTI hits $125 / $130 in September” — asks 15.8 / 9.5 for claims worth 64 / 36 on the paths where Brent touches 130 (and 12 / 7 unconditionally, next to the mids)

Idea added Sep 10, 2026View on Polymarket ↗
Resolves
Pyth 1-minute candles, CME active-month WTI, any high at or above the strike during a September trading session. Oct ’26 is the active month through the Sep 17 session; Nov ’26 from Sep 18 (6 PM ET Sep 17).
Where it is
WTI Oct settled 103.93 (high 104.44), Nov 99.51. $125 is +20% on Oct, +26% on Nov; $130 +25% / +31%.
Model, if Brent touches 130
$115 100% · $120 97% · $125 64% · $130 36% · $140 11%. The two regimes disagree most here (125: 70 at the full σ, 50 at 0.7×) because a low-vol path that touches 130 barely touches it; the mixture is what the page trades on.
Model, unconditional
$115 37 vs a 30.4 mid · $120 21 vs 22.2 · $125 12 vs 15.7 · $130 7 vs 9.1 · $140 2.1 vs 4.3. The model’s ladder is above the market in the body and below it in the tail — the market’s tail is fatter than either regime — and crosses it at the $120 rung (one point under the mid); the $125 / $130 rungs sit two to four points under. The $115 rung is the one with an unconditional edge (model 37 against a 30.4 mid) — held, 428.28 sh, no add above 34; on the others none is claimed, and the scenario is what the ticket buys.
Book
$125: 15.6 × 50 / 15.8 × 11 — $1,249,316 of offers, $1,570 of them under the conditional fair · $130: 8.7 × 12,111 / 9.5 × 30, $1,160 under fair · $120: 22.1 × 9 / 22.4 × 25, $10,627 under fair — the deepest of the three, but the account already owns 4,473.62 sh of it.
Reasoning

Every scenario dollar has to pass through this ladder, so it is where the roll matters most. Brent at 130 with the Oct contract still active (Sep 11–17, 17% of the touches) is a WTI print near 124–125; the same Brent print with Nov active is near 119–120, because the Nov contract trades $4.4 under Oct tonight and the whole curve is $5-a-month backwardated. That is why the $120 rung is worth 97 on the scenario but the $125 rung only 64: the second needs either an early touch or a Brent print well past 130 — and the median 130-path does go on to a 137 September high, which is why $130 WTI is still worth 36.

This is a pure scenario ticket: if Brent stalls at 115 every leg here expires worthless on Sep 30. The asymmetry is 4× on the scenario against −1× off it, on books that will fill — and the account’s own fills are in these books: the 20:34Z buy of 788.25 sh at 14.76¢ took the $125 touch to 15.8 × 11 with the next offer at 18.2, so the ticket pays 18–19 for what the account paid 14.8 two hours earlier. The spread is the load-bearing assumption and it is one day old: on Sep 9 Brent Nov settled $1.27 under WTI Oct and $2.81 over WTI Nov; the Sep 10 Brent-only spike (+8% against WTI’s +1.4%) took those to +$5.36 and +$9.78, which the model holds fixed; the Hyperliquid perps — a Brent index against a WTI index, not these contracts — ran $4.5–4.9 apart through August. If the quality spread halves back toward $3 the $125 rung is worth 85 rather than 70 at the full σ; at the perp’s $4.75 it is 74; if it reverts to $0 it is 98 — the honest conditional range on this rung is 64–98, and every case cuts in the buyer’s favour; the sensitivity table carries all four.

What can go wrong beyond the scenario failing: a Brent print of 130 on Sep 30 itself (the Nov contract’s expiry day) with WTI Nov at 118 pays nothing on either rung; Pyth’s feed, not CME’s settlement, is the resolution source (CME daily highs are the fallback only if Pyth is down); a spike that reverses inside the minute still counts if the 1-minute candle’s high printed it.

THE TICKET: Two legs, limits at the level shown: $125 YES ≤19¢ (15.8 × 11, 18.2 × 23, 18.3 × 50, 18.4 × 40, 18.5 × 2,000, 18.7 × 1,907, 18.8 × 3,839, 19 × 300 — 8,170 sh, $1,528); $130 YES ≤11¢ (9.5 × 30, 9.6 × 15, 10.3 × 20, 10.4 × 30, 10.5 × 30, 10.6 × 30, 10.7 × 86, 10.8 × 30, 10.9 × 230, 11 × 10,064 — 10,565 sh, $1,160). Size: $300 of the $1,050 basket ($150 a leg — about 811 and 1,364 shares at the limits); the levels above are what rests, not what to buy. The account is already $282 of cost long the same event one rung lower. Do not add to $120 above 25¢ — it is worth 21 without the scenario and the 33.2 × 28,757 wall is where the market says the book clears.
Value rank #1 by conditional RV among the resolvable-by-a-price rows; the roll is the whole argument.

#2 · THE CEASEFIRE BOOKS · NO · RV 2.4× / 1.9× “Israel × Iran ceasefire continues through Sep 30 / Oct 31” — NO at 16 / 27, worth 38 / 50 if Brent prints 130; “US × Iran effective ceasefire by Sep 30” NO at 26, worth 35

Idea added Sep 10, 2026View on Polymarket ↗
Resolves
Israel × Iran: NO if either side lands an air strike or surface-to-surface missile strike on the other’s territory by 11:59 PM IRST on the date (intercepts, naval fire, ground incursions and cyber do not count). US × Iran: YES needs a continuous 14-day period with no US air/missile strike on Iranian territory, starting by the date — strikes on tankers and ships at sea do not break it.
Where it is
The Israel–Iran ceasefire (since mid-July) is priced 84 to hold through Sep 30 and 74 through Oct 31; the US–Iran 14-day clock is priced 75 to complete by Sep 30 even though the two are trading strikes at sea this week.
Input, if Brent touches 130
The tab decomposes a $130 print into four drivers — a Gulf-infrastructure war (Houthi/Iranian strikes on Saudi, Qatari, Emirati energy assets) 40%; a direct US–Iran escalation on Iranian territory 30%; an Israel–Iran collapse 15%; a non-Iran cause (Bab el-Mandeb, Russia, a physical squeeze into the Nov expiry) 15% — and rates each book under each driver. Israel–Iran through Sep 30: 75 / 65 / 0 / 84 → 62. Through Oct 31: 60 / 50 / 0 / 73 → 50. US–Iran 14-day pause by Sep 30: 80 / 38 / 68 / 78 → 65 — shaded less than the others because the 14-day stretch has only to start by Sep 30 (a US strike on Sep 17 followed by quiet still resolves YES, and the book cannot settle before mid-October); the tab does not know the date of the last US strike on Iranian territory, and the sibling Sep-18 book at 70.5 says the market thinks a clock is already running.
Book
Sep 30: 84 × 6 / 85 × 8,223 — $67,983 of bids, $6,982 of NO under the conditional fair · Oct 31: 73 × 5 / 74 × 2,728, $11,338 under fair · US–Iran Sep 30: 74 × 4,284 / 76 × 3,437, $2,940. These are the deepest scenario books on the page by an order of magnitude.
Reasoning

The oil market is already trading the Gulf war: Brent is +22% in a month on Houthi strikes on Saudi facilities and a US–Iran exchange at sea, with the Israel–Iran ceasefire intact. A move from 109 to 130 in three weeks needs something the tape does not have yet, and every candidate is bad for these books — a strike on Saudi export infrastructure, a US strike on Iranian territory, Israeli strikes on Iranian energy assets. The one driver that leaves them alone (the 15% non-Iran bucket) is the one the March–September history makes least likely.

These are INPUT rows: the conditional numbers are stated, not simulated, and the honest range is wide — move the Israel–Iran weight from 15 to 30 and the Sep 30 conditional falls from 62 to about 49; move it to 5 and it rises to about 71. Even at 71 the NO at 16 is worth 29, a 1.8× claim. The direction is not in doubt; the size of the lift is — which is why these legs are capped in dollars below, not sized to the books.

What can go wrong: a $130 print driven by a Saudi–Houthi war that Iran keeps at arm’s length (the market’s Israel–Iran leg holds, the NO loses); a ceasefire that “continues” through Sep 30 on the resolution rules even after a strike that is intercepted; the Oct 31 leg has a full month of extra risk the scenario does not speak to. Unconditionally the tab has no view on any of these books — the market’s 84 / 73 / 75 are the inputs.

THE TICKET: Three legs: Israel × Iran through Sep 30 NO ≤19¢ (16 × 6, 17 × 3,944, 18 × 6,988, 19 × 9,993 — 20,931 sh, $3,828); through Oct 31 NO ≤30¢ (27 × 5, 28 × 641, 29 × 8,271, 30 × 2,875 — 11,792 sh, $3,442); US × Iran by Sep 30 NO ≤28¢ (26 × 4,284, 27 × 2,135, 28 × 979 — 7,398 sh, $1,964). Size: $400 of the $1,050 basket — $150 / $150 / $100 — the levels above are what rests ($3,828 / $3,442 / $1,964 walked), not what to buy; a stated input does not deserve a book-sized ticket.
Value rank #2 · the only scenario books deep enough to take size.

#3 · THE ESCALATION TELLS · RV 3.9× / 2.0× / 1.5× “Iran full airspace closure by Sep 30” YES at 9 (worth 35 on the scenario) · “Bab el-Mandeb effectively closed by Sep 30” YES at 9 (worth 18) · “Iran targets Saudi Arabia by Sep 30” YES at 25 (worth 37)

Idea added Sep 10, 2026View on Polymarket ↗
Resolves
Airspace: a general closure of the Tehran FIR to commercial flights (the Feb 28 and Jan 2026 closures qualify; the Jan 27 Hormuz-area notice and the VFR suspension do not). Bab el-Mandeb: IMF PortWatch 7-day average transits ≤ 10. Saudi / Qatar / Oman: an Iranian strike on that state’s territory.
Where it is
Airspace closure is priced 8.5 for September (32 by Dec 31); Bab el-Mandeb 8.8 (the Oct 31 and Dec 31 rungs 20 / 24); Iran-targets-Saudi 21.5, Qatar 18, Oman 5; Houthi action against Israel 6.1.
Input, if Brent touches 130
Airspace: Iran closed the Tehran FIR within hours on both prior occasions its territory was struck (Jan and Feb 28, 2026), so under the 30% US-strike driver and the 15% Israel driver it is likely — 60 / 65, raised from a first draft’s 45 / 55 on that precedent, and kept under 70 because a limited strike on a port or a naval base need not ground commercial aviation — modest under the Gulf-war driver (15), rare otherwise (6) → 35. Bab el-Mandeb 20 / 15 / 12 / 25 → 18. Iran-targets-Saudi 45 / 40 / 30 / 15 → 37; Qatar 35 / 35 / 25 / 15 → 30; Houthi-vs-Israel 15 / 12 / 30 / 6 → 15.
Book
Airspace: 8 × 4,911 / 9 × 514 — $15,135 of offers, $3,252 under fair · Bab el-Mandeb: 8.7 × 42 / 9 × 1,723, $1,468 under fair · Saudi: 18 × 82 / 25 × 45 — $455 of offers, a $25 idea · Houthi–Israel: 4.1 × 26 / 8.2 × 50, $235.
Reasoning

The airspace book is the cleanest tell on the page. It does not ask who fired or why; it asks whether Iranian territory was hit hard enough that Tehran grounded its own aviation, and that is what a $130 oil print most likely records. At 9 it is a 3.9× claim on the scenario and — unlike the ceasefire NOs — it is a YES you can size without lifting the price: $2,288 of offers sit within five points of the touch and $3,252 under the conditional fair (out to 18).

Bab el-Mandeb is the one leg that pays under the non-Iran driver too (a Red Sea closure is itself a $130 story), which is why its 15% bucket carries a 25 rather than a 6. The Saudi and Qatar target books are the purest expression of the Gulf-war driver but the Saudi book has $25 of offers under fair — it is priced, not tradeable.

What can go wrong: Iran closes airspace for a reason unrelated to a strike (weather and quakes are excluded, but a pre-emptive closure ahead of an expected attack still needs to be “general”); the PortWatch 7-day average lags a closure by up to a week, so a late-September Red Sea event may not print ≤ 10 until October — the Oct 31 rung at 21 (worth 28) is the safer version of the same claim.

THE TICKET: Three legs: airspace closure YES ≤12¢ (9 × 514, 10 × 4,067, 11 × 4,665, 12 × 7,870 — 17,116 sh, $1,911); Bab el-Mandeb Sep 30 YES ≤9.2¢ (9 × 1,723, 9.1 × 4,611, 9.2 × 1,437 — 7,771 sh, $707); Houthi-vs-Israel YES ≤10¢ (8.2 × 50, 8.5 × 40, 9.6 × 92, 9.7 × 700, 10 × 469 — 1,351 sh, $131). Skip the Saudi and Qatar books unless a $200 offer appears. Size: $150 of the basket across the three.

Reasoning

The oil–equity beta is the best-measured number on this tab, and it is not small: −0.15% of S&P per 1% of Brent, on 176 days, R² 0.40. A move from 109 to 130 is +17% in logs, which is −2.6% of index on the beta alone before the noise; the conditional paths get there with a 7,260 low. The September SPY-LOW rungs are priced off a normal month — $720 at 17 — and they are the cheapest way on the page to own the equity side of an oil shock.

The Treasuries tab found the same books CHEAP on Sep 2 and the account bought the $750 rung at 48.6¢ and sold it at 40¢; the index has since fallen from 762 to 759 and the $750 book has gone bidless above 62. Every Relevant Market, Re-Priced on the Paths Where Brent Touches 130

124 rows · 123 books walked Sep 10 22:17 / 22:53 UTC · ranked by conditional RV (better side), then capturable dollars P = the tab’s unconditional probability (MODEL rows: the two-regime bootstrap, equal-weighted; LIFT rows: the model’s own number, shown for reference only — the conditional fair on those rows is the market mid updated in odds space by the model’s likelihood ratio [P if 130 ÷ (1 − P if 130)] ÷ [P ÷ (1 − P)], which is normalised by construction; INPUT rows: the market mid). P if 130 = the same event measured on the paths that touch 130 (MODEL / LIFT, regimes weighted 71 / 29 by how often each touches) or the stated input (INPUT). Lift = P if 130 ÷ P (on LIFT rows, cond fair ÷ mid). Cond fair = the value of the better side on the scenario; Ask = what that side costs at the touch (NO ask = 100 − YES bid); RV if 130 = cond fair ÷ ask. Capturable = dollars of that side resting anywhere under the conditional fair, walked level by level at 22:53 UTC — it is fill cost, not edge, and a deep book one point under fair counts in full (the DEEP badge, not this column, is the depth claim). Rows with a bid–ask spread over 15 points are badged WIDE: the mid is not a price there and no SCENARIO BUY is issued on them; LIFT rows whose model P is outside 5–95 are badged TAIL and get no ticket. The odds-space update moves every LIFT row in the direction of the scenario — the 5.2% rung’s fair is 52 here against 46 under a plain ratio — which is the correct update if the model’s ratio is right and a larger error if it is not. Mids refresh live where the token is registered; everything else is the Sep 10 walk.

The emergency-cut input is lower than the market, not higher: it is bounded by the no-cuts input, and a crash tail is priced in the S&P rows instead. Read across. The scenario probability is the number that moves most (26.6 at the March-heavy σ, 10.7 at the recent σ) and it is exactly the number the ticket does not need: a scenario basket is priced on the conditionals. Among those, the WTI rungs above 125 and the crude-ATH lift are regime-sensitive (a low-vol path that touches 130 barely touches it — 125 goes 70 → 50, 130 goes 42 → 20), which is why the page’s numbers are the touch-weighted mixture and why the $140 rung is not traded; the calendar-spread κ moves the 125 rung by ±3 and a quality spread that halves back to $3 (it was $1–2 in early September) lifts it to 85 at the full σ — the single biggest lever on card #1; the 10-year beta moves the September rates rungs by ±10–15 and nothing else; the S&P beta moves the SPY rungs by ±10 at the near strikes and ±20 at $720. The gold, silver and dollar conditionals hardly move across variants because their betas are not varied — the honest range there is the t-statistic, not the table. The last row is the one to read twice: every conditional on this page is measured on the whole path, and a bootstrap without mean reversion keeps Brent near 130 once it has touched it (median Sep 30 close 130); on the 19% of touch-paths that retrace to a Sep 30 close under 120 — the March 9 shape, 117.58 high and a 91 close — the S&P ends near 7,576, the 10-year near 4.96, and the SPY-$720 touch is 26% rather than 38. The WTI rungs, which resolve on the touch, do not care; the cross-asset legs do, and the basket weights them accordingly. Not modelled: a jump at the Sep 16 FOMC (the rates ladder is oil plus i.i.d. noise; the Fed inputs live in a separate table) and volatility clustering (the bootstrap is i.i.d.; the two regimes are the substitute). Calendar: 14 ICE/CME sessions Sep 11–30 (the Nov Brent contract expires Sep 30; Oct 1 is Dec ’26 at a $5 discount and is not modelled as a separate touch); WTI active month Oct ’26 through the Sep 17 session, Nov ’26 from Sep 18; weekend perp moves are folded into Monday’s session high and low; 14 Treasury prints; 62 more Treasury business days to Dec 31 (ex Oct 12, Nov 11, Nov 26, Dec 25) for the before-2027 rungs.

What would falsify this tab

Three commitments. (1) If Brent touches 130 by Oct 1 and the WTI-$120 rung does not resolve YES, the roll model is wrong in the direction that matters: the fixed $5.36 quality spread is retired for a spread re-estimated on the ICE and CME settlements of the spike (the lever the sensitivity table shows is the quality spread, not κ). (2) If Brent touches 130 and the S&P closes Sep 30 above 7,700 — higher than tonight’s 7,592, an outcome the model gives well under 10% even on the touch-and-retrace subset (median 7,576; the all-paths median is 7,403) — the oil–equity beta is not usable for conditional pricing at a three-week horizon and the SPY rungs come off future scenario books. (3) The Iran inputs are scored as a set: if Brent touches 130 and none of the four escalation tells (airspace closure, a Saudi or Qatari strike, a Bab el-Mandeb closure, an Israel–Iran strike) prints by Oct 15, the four-driver decomposition over-weighted the Iran channel and the next scenario book runs the non-Iran driver at 40%. And one that cannot be scored by outcome: the scenario is 18.6% here and about 24% at the market’s WTI-125 mid pushed through the roll mapping; if the tab’s scenario baskets are bought at that rate for a year and the scenarios arrive at less than half it, the mixture’s full-σ regime is over-weighted. Snapshot built Sep 10–11, 2026 on the Sep 10 settlements — the first walk after the day’s +8% print. Reviewed three times before publication (a model attack, a fact-check and a trader’s read, three rounds each); the review moved the WTI $125 / $130 fairs from 60 / 33 to 64 / 36 (the spread decomposition), the airspace input from 29 to 35, the SPY rungs down 3–4 points (the ladder’s own implied vol), re-solved the Fed set, replaced the LIFT ratio with an odds-space update, and corrected the basket’s break-even from a mis-stated 12% to 28%. Fictitious research page; nothing here is investment advice.

CHEAP the market price is below the model fair — the contract is undervalued, and these are the bets to make. Edge is negative because edge = mid − fair.RICH the market price is above fair — overvalued. If you hold it, that is a trim signal; if you do not, this page will not short it just because the model says so.FAIR inside ±2.5 points of fair — nothing to do.TAIL mid under 2¢ and fair under 0.5 — no model resolution; quoted for context and depth only.Value rank answers “which of these can I actually act on, and for how much?” — BUY ranks the CHEAP rows by capturable edge (Σ(fair − ask) × size over the ask levels under fair); TRIM ranks the RICH rows the account already owns. Everything else is unranked, with the reason in the cell.

Sensitivity. The σ is the whole model. At σ 2.0 / 2.35 / 3.0 the Dec $100k leg is 27.1 / 34.9 / 46.3, the Dec $90k leg 53.3 / 59.6 / 67.8, the Dec $60k dip 22.6 / 30.3 / 42.0 (every August fair is 0.0 at all three — the σ argument is over for that ladder). At σ 2.0 (nearest the 60-day realised of 1.93 and the collapsed 10-day of 1.52) the up-ladder’s deep CHEAPs compress but survive — $90k −6.3, $95k −4.0, $100k −3.6 — while $110k (+0.9) and $85k (−1.0) go FAIR and the $60k dip flips RICH (+3.9); the capturable trio collapses to $223 / $124 / $113 on the $95k / $100k / $90k. At σ 3.0 every up-rung through $120k is CHEAP by double digits and even the RICH dip belt inverts — $60k −15.5, $55k −6.0, $50k −3.0 all CHEAP, only $35k/$30k staying RICH. The windows: 10d 1.52%, 20d 2.61%, 30d 2.21%, 60d 1.93%, 90d 2.00%, 250d 2.42%, 365d 2.30%. The house keeps 2.35 because the December horizon is 122 days and the short windows have just demonstrated their whole failure mode in one fortnight (3.31 → 1.52) — but that is a choice, and the table’s verdicts are its consequence. What the model does not price: drift, regime change, and the Binance/Coinbase basis. Capturable edge walks the raw ask side up to the σ 2.35 fair and sums (fair − ask) × size level by level.

Methodology, Sources & Honesty Box

The touch model

Driftless lognormal, reflection principle: P(touch B before T) = 2·N(−|ln(B/S)| / (σ√T)), S = $78,414.25 (Coinbase BTC-USD, 01:27 UTC Sep 1), σ in %/day, T in days. Symmetric by construction — the same formula prices a reach and a dip — and driftless by choice, because no drift estimate on Bitcoin has a t-statistic worth publishing. The model is the same first-passage machinery the Treasuries tab uses without the barrier shift: these markets resolve on 1-minute candles, so the continuous-monitoring assumption is close to exact.

T, and what the clock does

T_aug = 0.11 days (≈2.5 hours), to Aug 31 23:59 ET = Sep 1 04:00Z; T_dec = 122.1 days, to Dec 31 23:59 ET = Jan 1 05:00Z; both measured from the 01:27Z Sep 1 walk. Fairs are baked at those T and do not decay on the page. As the clock runs the true touch probability falls while the baked fair stays put, so a stale bake flatters every live CHEAP badge and under-reports every RICH one. The August question is settled — at 2.5 hours every August fair rounds to 0.0 and the rows are frozen outright. For December the decay is slow but real (the anchor’s fair loses roughly 0.2 pt per stale day); re-bake at every run.

σ, and its sensitivity

House σ = 2.35%/day, baked from the full-history close-to-close realised at the Aug 21 build (≈45% annualised); the fresh 365-day read is 2.30 and the 250-day 2.42, so the house number still sits inside the long-window band. Alternatives measured at this walk: 10d 1.52%, 20d 2.61%, 30d 2.21%, 60d 1.93%, 90d 2.00% — the 10-day’s collapse from 3.31 in one week is the argument against short windows made by the windows themselves. The σ 2.0 and σ 3.0 columns in the data bracket every fair in the table; the row notes print the implied σ — the daily vol at which the model reproduces the mid — so the reader can see which σ the market is using rather than argue about which one the page should. Every verdict is a statement about 2.35 vs that number.

Binance vs Coinbase

All 51 markets resolve on the Binance BTC/USDT 1-minute candle high (reach) or low (dip). Spot, candles and realised vol on this page are Coinbase BTC-USD. Binance USDT prints typically run a few tens of dollars above Coinbase USD; the page discloses and does not adjust. It mattered most for the one resolution the ladders have produced — the Aug $80k reach, where Coinbase’s Aug 24 daily high stopped at 79,999.99 — one cent shy — while Binance printed the level and settled the market. One more rule that matters, verbatim from the market descriptions: each market counts Binance candles “from the creation of this market” and “price action before this market’s creation will not be considered” — the August ladder listed Aug 21 16:17Z, mid-rip, which is why the month’s pre-listing $62,210 low never touched the dip legs and all of them die NO tonight.

The 1–2¢ tail floor

Rows with mid < 2.0¢ and fair < 0.5 are labelled TAIL and publish no edge. The implied σ of 3–10%/day on those rows (Dec $5k dip 9.73%, Dec $1M reach 8.30%, Dec $10k dip 7.98%) is the price of warehousing an unsellable contract, not a vol forecast. Ten December rows wear TAIL tonight (the $170k–$1M reaches and the $20k/$10k/$5k dips), and the floors even print INVERTED down there ($15k over $20k, $190k over $180k) — noise, not information. The Dec $25k dip (2.45¢, +2.4) and the $15k dip (2.05¢) sit just above the threshold and wear FAIR; they are floor pricing too. The twenty live August rows are past even that: bidless, frozen, unpollable.

Books, and capturable edge

Every quote is a CLOB /book snapshot with asset_id matched to the market’s YES token, all 51 books walked 01:26–01:27Z Sep 1 with every timestamp seconds-fresh at the fetch. Can buy = the full ask side in dollars, Can sell = the full bid side; Market? is DEEP / OK / THIN / NO MARKET on those. Capturable edge for a CHEAP row = Σ(fair − askᵢ) × sizeᵢ over every ask level priced under the σ 2.35 fair, from the raw book — what a buyer walking the offer up to fair would pocket at fair: $100k $2,660, $95k $2,337, $90k $1,703, $110k $795, $60k dip $514, $85k $146. Walk-outs for the five held legs are from the same books: all five fill in full, $3,166.25 against a $3,290.30 mark.

What the model cannot do

It has no drift: a +25% five-session move is, to the model, a draw from a zero-mean distribution, and the next five are too. It has no regime: the SEC Aug 18 / White House Aug 19 / CFTC Aug 20 sequence is a level shift in the rule set, and the model treats Aug 21 like any other day at 2.35%. It has no skew of its own, which is precisely why it can see the market’s: up 1.73–2.24, down 2.64–4.60. The skew is a claim — the market’s claim that the rip mean-reverts — and this page reports it rather than trading against it. Twelve CHEAP/RICH badges on the December ladder are one disagreement about σ, repeated.

Sources

Coinbase BTC-USD spot, 24h stats and daily candles (through the Sep 1 partial) and CoinGecko 365-day dailies for the long realised · Polymarket CLOB /book and /midpoint for all 51 legs, plus gamma-api for market rules and the (absent) September listing; data-api /positions, /activity and /value for the account — this walk’s fetches ran through the reader’s own browser after the autodata pipeline stalled, every book validated on asset_id and timestamp · listing-day context (Yahoo/Motley Fool, Aug 21) and the Aug 18–20 policy sequence as previously reported. Live refresh now makes 29 BTC CLOB midpoint calls per 60 s — the twenty frozen August rows and the two RESOLVED rows no longer poll. Fictitious research page — not financial advice.

What would falsify this tab

A Dec up-rung mid rising to its σ 2.35 fair with spot unchanged — the market adopting the house σ — would make the skew disappear and the CHEAP badges with it; that is the test of the claim, and it is the market’s to pass. Beyond that, tonight’s specific commitments: (1) no BTC adds at any rung while the family is over 20% of the book — the tighter line the cards have used since Aug 22, restated here after the account traded through it (row 256); (2) re-walk all five bid sides every run and print the haircut; (3) the September monthly ladder joins this page the run after Polymarket lists it; (4) the frozen August rows drop from the table at the first run after resolution posts.

Iran — The Ground-Invasion Book

What would be the top bets on Polymarket if the United States launched a ground invasion of Iran? This tab is the answer, priced: a sweep of the whole site (03:14 UTC Sep 1, 2026 — ~150 events surveyed, 43 books walked with asset_id and timestamp validation) scored against ONE hypothetical scenario — a US ground offensive to take and hold Iranian territory, launched this month. The market that IS the scenario trades: “Will the US invade Iran before 2027” prices 15.5¢ on a half-million-dollar book — resolution: “a military offensive intended to establish control over any portion of Iran” — and every figure here is CONDITIONAL on that 15.5% event firing. The backdrop is already a war ladder: the Israel–Iran ceasefire holds at 86/76.5/67 (Sep/Oct/Dec), Hormuz traffic is NOT normal (2.8¢ by Sep 30, 28.5¢ by Dec 31), Iran-targets-UAE prints ~94 on its September rungs (sweep prices, not book-walked), the September WTI ladder prices a $90 touch at 71.5¢, and the succession is unsettled — Mojtaba Khamenei prices 83¢ to be leader at year-end but only 21.5¢ to make a public appearance by then. Against that base, the top conditional tickets rank: the trigger itself (15.5 → ~97, 6.1×, the deepest book on the board), Kharg Island by Sep 30 at 2.4¢ (14.6×), the WTI $110/$120 September rungs (12–17×), Iran full-airspace closure at 9¢ (9.4×), Israel closing its own airspace at 6¢ (9.2×), the ceasefire obituary (NO at 15¢, 6×), and the uranium-seizure sleeper at 6¢ (5×). A $1,000 basket WALKED into the actual ladders (thin legs fill above their touches) is worth ≈$6,776 conditional on invasion — and ≈$924 at the market’s own odds; the ≈8% gap is bid–ask spread, full stop: the page claims torque, not free money. No trades are placed from this tab. Fictitious research page — not financial advice.

The $1,000 basket
Thirteen legs, each WALKED into its ladder rather than priced at a touch that cannot fill ($400 trigger @16¢ / $100 ceasefire-Sep NO @15¢ / $50+$50 Kharg Sep@2.4¢+Dec@8¢ / $75 Iran-airspace @9¢ / $50 WTI-100 @19.8¢ avg + $25 WTI-110 @5.8¢ + $25 WTI-120 @2.5¢ / $50 uranium seizure @6¢ / $50 Israel-airspace @6.9¢ avg / $50 emergency cut @8¢ / $50 gold-$6k @13¢ / $25 Mojtaba-leader NO @17.7¢ avg): conditional value ≈$6,776 (6.8×). If no invasion comes, the trigger, Kharg, airspace and ceasefire legs go to ≈zero and the basket is worth a few hundred dollars of surviving oil/gold/cut optionality.
The traps
Five bets that FEEL like invasion bets and mostly aren’t: US recession by Dec 31 (the determination lags the war by quarters — 7.5¢ is a clock bet, not a war bet) · draft authorized in 2026 (no draft since 1973; 4.4¢ needs an act of Congress in four months) · “peace talks” NO (surrender talks are still talks — invasion can resolve this YES) · countries-struck “9” (an exact bucket, and Iran is already in the count) · regime falls by Dec 31 (the resolution bar is dissolution of core structures — Baghdad 2003 took three weeks; Tehran-wide collapse inside four months is the 25% case, not the base case).

#2 · KHARG — THE FIRST OBJECTIVE 2.4¢ SEP / 8¢ DEC · 14.6× / 7.5× The island that loads ~90% of Iran’s crude exports, priced at 2.3/7.5 to be OUT of Iranian control — the highest real multiple on the board, against the strictest resolution rule on it

Scenario exhibit · Sep 1, 2026 View on Polymarket ↗

A ground campaign against Iran starts where the oil leaves: Kharg is small, offshore, and strategically decisive — the classic day-one amphibious objective. The September rung at 2.4¢ pays 14.6× on $13k of real asks; December at 8¢ pays 7.5×. The catch is the rule: “another state, occupying force, or internationally backed authority has ESTABLISHED control — raids, bombardment, naval presence, contested control do not qualify.” The desk’s 35%/60% conditionals price exactly that: taking the island fast is likely; the resolver seeing “established control” inside the month is the risk being paid 14.6× to hold. The four-island basket variant (Farsi/Hengam/Hormuz/Kharg by Sep 30, 3.3¢) takes rank #3 in the table on the mechanical rule — but $2.97 rests at its touch, so the rank is nominal and no card is built on it.

THE TICKET: None. The Sep/Dec pair is the board’s cleanest torque-vs-rule tradeoff: 2.4¢ buys the fast-campaign case, 8¢ buys the campaign, and both die worthless on airstrikes-only.

The desk prices that at ~10% and notes it is the difference between 6× and the trigger’s clean 6.1×: same multiple, more moving parts — which is the whole ranking argument in one line.

THE TICKET: None. For a size-constrained board (and this one is — see the table’s Can-buy column), ceasefire NO is where a second thousand dollars would actually fit.

#6 · THE SEIZURE SLEEPER 6¢ · 5× · THE OBJECTIVE MARKET “US obtains Iranian enriched uranium by Dec 31” at 5 mid — the market prices it as dead diplomacy, but securing the stockpile is a STATED objective of any ground operation, and capture counts as obtaining

Scenario exhibit · Sep 1, 2026 View on Polymarket ↗

Two uranium markets, opposite exposures: Iran-AGREES-to-surrender (6.5 mid) is a diplomacy market that an invasion kills — while US-OBTAINS (5 mid) is agnostic about HOW — the desk ASSUMES capture counts as obtaining; this rule text was not pulled in the sweep, so the 30% conditional carries that unverified assumption. An invasion flips the second from a dead-deal residue into a war objective with a 30% desk conditional — 5× on $8.2k of asks. The pair is this page’s favorite exhibit of scenario work done properly: two markets a screen apart, near-identical prices, and the invasion moves them in OPPOSITE directions.

THE TICKET: None. The spread (long OBTAINS / the surrender leg dies on its own) is the sophisticated version; the 6¢ outright is the simple one.

#7 · THE MACRO KICKERS EMERGENCY CUT 8¢ (4.4×) · GOLD $6K 13¢ (2.7×) · SPX/BTC AMBIGUOUS The Fed does not schedule wars: an intermeeting cut at 8¢ is the cleanest macro expression; gold’s $6,000 rung the second; the equity-crash rungs are thin and the BTC channel is a coin-flip

Scenario exhibit · Sep 1, 2026 View on Polymarket ↗

The macro chain — oil shock → risk-off → Fed reaction — prices at: emergency cut before 2027 7.5 mid (35% conditional, 4.4×); gold $6,000 by Dec 12.5 (35%, 2.7×) with $7,000 at 5.5 (12%, 2.0×); SPX-touches-5,800 8.5 (30%, 3.0× — it takes rank #20 on the mechanical rule and a $59 book takes no real money). Two honest caveats: an oil-shock war is INFLATIONARY, which cuts against the cut (hence 35%, not 60%), and this site’s own Treasuries tab has the hike complex at 50+ — an invasion scrambles that tab’s whole board, which is disclosed there, not re-priced here. Notably absent from the top bets: Bitcoin — the desk has no conviction on the war-BTC sign and says so rather than inventing one.

THE TICKET: None. The cut is the macro line that pays on the WAR STARTING; everything else macro pays on how it goes.

#8 · THE TRAPS — WHAT NOT TO BUY FIVE INTUITIVE BETS THAT MOSTLY AREN’T Recession (a clock trap) · the draft (a base-rate trap) · peace-talks NO (a definition trap) · countries-struck “9” (a bucket trap) · regime-fall (a bar trap) — each looks like the trade and each mostly isn’t

Scenario exhibit · Sep 1, 2026 View on Polymarket ↗

Recession by Dec 31 (7.5¢): even a war-shock recession that starts in October is not DECLARED by December — the market’s clock beats the economy’s; desk conditional 12%, multiple 1.5×. Draft authorized (4.4¢): requires Congress; hasn’t happened since 1973; an all-volunteer invasion force is the entire modern doctrine — 8%. Peace-talks NO: the intuition says war kills talks; the rule says a surrender negotiation IS a round of talks — the invasion can resolve this market YES, and the desk scores the NO side 1.2×, i.e. dead money. Countries-struck “9” (30¢): an exact bucket where Iran is already in the count — the invasion itself adds NOTHING, spillover can blow through 9 to 10+, and the desk keeps its conditional AT the market’s own ~30. Regime falls (7.5¢): the bar is dissolution of the Supreme Leader’s office, the Guardian Council AND IRGC control by Dec 31 — the desk’s 25% is a fast-collapse bet, and 3.1× is thin pay for it next to Kharg’s 7.5× for taking one island.

THE TICKET: None — emphatically. The traps section exists because “what would pay on an invasion” and “what FEELS like it would pay” diverge by more, in this complex, than anywhere else on the site.

Eight cards, one hypothetical. The discipline that survives contact with the whole board: the best invasion bet is the invasion market (6.1×, definitional, $85k deep), and every higher multiple on the page — Kharg’s 14.6×, the WTI rungs’ 12–17×, airspace’s 9.4× — is paid for taking a specific risk the trigger doesn’t carry: a resolver’s judgment of “established control,” a strike-price’s distance, a NOTAM’s timing. The $1,000 basket (13 legs, walked into the ladders — the thin legs fill ABOVE their touches: WTI-100 averages 19.8¢, the $120 rung 2.5¢, Israel-airspace 6.9¢) carries conditional value ≈$6,776 against ≈$924 at the market’s own odds — torque, not edge, and the gap between $1,000 in and $924 marked is bid–ask spread, stated plainly. The account trades none of it; the scenario itself is the market’s 15.5% event, not the desk’s forecast.

Sensitivity. The conditionals are the whole model. Halve the Kharg-Sep conditional (35% → 17.5%) and its 14.6× becomes 7.3× — still ahead of the trigger; cut the airspace pair to 60/35 and the Israel leg (5.8×) drops below the trigger while Iran-Sep still clears it at 6.7×. The rankings that survive ANY defensible re-estimate: the trigger’s 6.1× (definitional), the ceasefire family’s 3–6× (a US ground war that leaves the Israel–Iran ceasefire “continuing” needs a lawyer, not an analyst), and the traps (each fails on its own rule or clock, not on a probability). The one number that moves everything and appears in exactly one cell of the table (the trigger’s own mid): P(invasion) itself — the market says 15.5%, and every YES ticket here is, unconditionally, a bet that 15.5 is too low, bought at the multiple shown.

Methodology, Sources & Honesty Box

What this tab is — and is not

A scenario screen, built to answer one question: which existing Polymarket markets reprice most if the US launches a ground invasion of Iran. It is NOT a forecast that the invasion happens (the market prices that at 15.5%), NOT a trade slate (the account places nothing from this tab), and NOT a model in the Treasuries/Bitcoin sense — there is no distribution being priced, only one conditional branch. The styling and disciplines are borrowed from the Treasuries tab; the epistemics are weaker and labeled as such.

The conditionals

Every P(YES|invasion) is a desk estimate, assigned market-by-market against each market’s RESOLUTION TEXT (not its title), assuming the offensive launches in September 2026. The load-bearing ones: trigger ≈97 (definitional, minus resolver risk) · Kharg Sep/Dec 35/60 (the “established control” bar) · airspace 85/95/55 (near-mechanical) · WTI 85/60/40/12 ($150 requires Hormuz closure) · ceasefire survives Sep 10 (the Israel×Iran letter-of-the-market caveat) · regime falls 25 (the dissolution bar) · recession 12 (the determination clock). Attack the numbers — the table re-ranks under yours; the sensitivity note names which rankings survive.

Sources & plumbing

Market sweep: gamma-api public-search across ~40 query terms plus event pulls, ~150 unique events surveyed, 43 shortlisted. Books: CLOB /book for every shortlisted YES token, walked 03:14 UTC Sep 1, 2026 through the reader’s own browser (the autodata Action is down — same fallback as the Sep 1 Bitcoin bake), each validated on asset_id and a fresh timestamp. Resolution rules quoted from the market descriptions (invasion, Kharg, regime-fall verbatim in the cards). Prices are cents; mid = (best bid + best ask)/2. This tab does not refresh live and its numbers date from the walk — a deliberate choice for a scenario exhibit.

What would falsify this tab

(1) An invasion that fires WITHOUT the top bets paying — a Kharg campaign the resolver never scores, an air war with open skies, a ceasefire that legally “continues” — each would convict a specific conditional, and the table names which. (2) The trigger market resolving YES on something that is not a ground invasion (its text needs only “a military offensive intended to establish control”) — in that branch the airspace/Kharg legs underperform their conditionals and the trigger still pays; the ranking’s first line survives. (3) Polymarket listing a cleaner scenario market (an explicit “US ground forces in Iran” contract) — this page re-anchors to it the run after it lists. Fictitious research page — not financial advice.

Decision Tracking — Scoring Every Executed Call

When a recommendation from this site gets actioned (add-on, new position, or sell), it moves here as a permanent ledger entry. Each row is re-scored live against the current market so the effectiveness of every decision is measurable — sells score the money saved by exiting, adds score P&L since the fill. The twice-daily run appends new executions with actual average fills from the trade history.

How scoring works — SELLS: Since Decision = (exit price − current price) × shares. Positive means the exit saved money (the position kept falling); negative means it left money on the table so far. Final verdicts land at resolution. ADDS/BUYS: Since Decision = (current − fill) × shares, plus realized payout at resolution. Add-side executions are detected and appended automatically by the twice-daily run from the account's trade history — with actual average fills replacing estimates.
